What you need

Before you start a chapter, have these to hand.

  • A Root, the end module: it gives the units their power and mixes their sound together, and your headphones plug into it.
  • Step, the sequencer. It plays the notes: everything in this book is written on Step and played by it.
  • The units each chapter asks for, joined in a row to the right of the Root. Each chapter says which near its start, and the table below gathers them all. The first two chapters of music, techno and acid, need only three: Step, Strike (drums) and Volt (bass).
  • Headphones, or speakers, with an ordinary 3.5 mm plug, into the Root's PHONES socket.

You don't need to own every unit in the table. Every unit is the same box until you choose what it becomes, and you can change it as often as you like: flash a unit as Taste for the hip-hop chapter, then as Grit for ambient. Your sounds aren't lost when you do: they're kept kind by kind, so when you flash it back as Taste, your Taste sounds are there, just as you left them. The Quick Start guide in the box says how to flash a unit.

ChapterYou'll need, with Step and the Root
3 TechnoStrike, Volt. Haze and Glass are optional.
4 AcidStrike, Volt. Haze is optional.
5 HouseStrike, Volt, Ember or Glass, Haze.
6 Hip-hopTaste, Strike, Volt, and for Track 3 a microphone (or the one built into the Root).
7 AmbientGlass, Grit, Haze, and Axis for Track 3 (or Glass alone).
8 Jungle and drum and bassTaste, Strike, Volt, Haze.
9 Synth-pop and synthwaveGlass, Ember, Axis, Volt, Strike, Haze.
10 Step from start to finishAny one synth to play.
11 Playing livePilot, and the units of any chapter before it.

Optional

  • A MIDI keyboard, for playing parts in by hand and for trying ideas out. Any keyboard with a MIDI OUT socket will do (which cable, below).
  • A microSD card in the Root, for backing up your songs and sounds, and for loading samples.
  • A computer, for updating the firmware, and for recording what you make: the Root's LINE OUT goes into a computer's audio input, and its MIDI OUT sends Step's notes and clock to music software.
  • Making Sounds, the companion to this book, for when you want to build your own sounds instead of choosing the factory ones.

Which keyboard, and which cable

The Root's MIDI IN is a small 3.5 mm socket, like a headphone socket. Plenty of small keyboards have exactly that socket for their MIDI OUT, and a plain 3.5 mm stereo cable joins them. Bigger keyboards have the big round five-pin MIDI OUT socket instead, so you'll need an adapter: a "TRS MIDI Type A" one, which is the commonest kind.

A keyboard with only a USB socket

Look for a keyboard with a MIDI OUT socket. Most small ones get their power from their USB socket, and any phone charger or power bank will do for that: no computer needed.

A keyboard that only has USB can't plug straight into the Root: the Root's USB socket is for a computer (and for the power). Plug the keyboard into a computer, and the computer into the Root, and the computer passes the notes on. Or use a small "USB MIDI host" box, which turns a USB keyboard's notes into an ordinary MIDI OUT.

Before you start - how tracks are made

Most of the music you dance to was made by one person, in a small room, on a few boxes like these.

Put on almost any electronic track and listen to it closely. Underneath, it's surprisingly simple: a drum pattern a bar or two long, a bass line about the same length, perhaps a chord or a hook, all going round and round. What makes it a piece of music rather than a loop is what happens to those few parts over five or six minutes: one drops out and comes back, a filter opens, a delay builds, everything stops for a moment and then crashes back in. That's the hidden craft in this book's title. It isn't writing long tunes; it's knowing what to leave out, and when.

That's also why so much of this music was made by people with no formal training and very little money. Detroit techno and Chicago house were made by teenagers and young DJs on second-hand drum machines nobody else wanted. Jungle was made on cheap samplers in bedrooms. Nobody gave them permission, and few of them had lessons. They learned by doing: they copied the records they loved, worked out by ear how they were made, got it wrong in interesting ways, and kept what worked. Many of them came to know a great deal about music that way, and so will you.

This book does the same thing, with a little more help. Each chapter of music takes one style, tells you where it came from, and then builds three tracks in it with you, each one a step further than the last: the first straight from a recipe, the second with changes, and the third with your own choices. By the end you'll have made techno, acid, house, hip-hop, ambient, jungle and synthwave, and you'll know what makes each one what it is.

These tracks are not the point

Of course, none of the tracks in this book is held up as a great piece of music. In some ways they're the opposite: each one is about the most ordinary, conservative example of its style we could make, so that nothing in it gets in the way of what it's there to show you, and so that your own ideas have a plain, sturdy frame to hang on. Please don't copy them slavishly. That's not because you'd need our permission: you don't, and you never will. It's because you'll come up with much better things yourself.

How to use this book

Chapter 1 is how every unit works, the same whatever it is, and chapter 2 is a short history of electronic music, from the first electronic instruments to the dance floor. Then come the chapters of music, and they're meant to be read in order: each one teaches you something new on Step, and builds on the chapter before. Techno teaches the basics, acid adds accents and slides, house adds chords and whole songs, and so on.

Two ways through

The chapters of music teach Step a little at a time, as each kind of music needs it, so you're making music from the first page. If you'd rather learn how a tool works before you use it, chapter 10 is Step from start to finish, page by page. Read it first if you like, then come back to chapter 3. Either way works: it's your choice.

Every track uses the units' factory sounds, so you can hear exactly what the book describes. Once a track works, change the sounds: it's the quickest way to make it your own, and Making Sounds, the companion to this book, shows you how to build your own from scratch.

Instrument names in this book (such as TR-808, TR-909 and TB-303, which belong to Roland Corporation, Minimoog, which belongs to Moog Music, and DX7, which belongs to Yamaha Corporation) are trademarks of their owners. They're mentioned for their history. Tessel isn't connected with any of these companies or endorsed by them.

Chapter 1 - Getting around

Everything that's the same on every unit. Learn it once.

Every Tessel unit is the same box. The screen is in the same place, the four encoders are in the same place, the keys run down the same side, and the buttons that matter most, SOUNDS and SETUP, sit in the same spots. What changes from one unit to the next is what the buttons are called and what they do. So this chapter is about the box, and about joining several of them together, which is how music gets made.

If you've read Making Sounds, most of this chapter will be familiar: skim it, and read sections 1.8 and 1.9, which are new. If you haven't, have a unit in front of you as you read: everything here is quicker to learn by doing than by reading.

1.1 How this book tells you what to press

Most of this book is instructions of the "press this, then turn that" kind, and writing them out in full sentences gets tiring for everybody very quickly. So instead they're written as a little strip of coloured shapes, in the order you do them. Here's one:

VCF›2RES›5.0

That reads: press the button marked VCF, then turn encoder 2 (the box on the screen it changes is called RES) until it says 5.0. Every route in the book is built from the same few pieces:

VCFA button: press it. White with a small dark square, like a button on the panel's white strip.
VECTORVECTOR ENVA button with a page name on it: press the button until the bar along the top of the screen says that name. Some buttons have two pages, and pressing again flips between them, so you might need one press or two. The name in the pill is the name you'll see at the top of the screen.
CHORUSagainPress a button again to switch something on or off rather than to change page.
holdOCT+Hold a button down.
2RESAn encoder, by its number, and the name of the box on the screen it changes: turn it.
push1Push an encoder, like a button, and let go.
hold4Hold an encoder pushed in until the bar on the screen fills up.
5.0The value to set, written exactly as the screen shows it.
C3A key, by its note.

With several units on the go, a route starts by saying which unit it's on, in capitals: on STRIKE, PUNCH.

Apart from the routes, there are three kinds of box, and they always mean the same thing.

Try this

Something to do with your hands. These are the most important part of the book, and they're short.

Watch out

A trap, or something that surprises nearly everybody the first time.

Keep

Something worth remembering after you've closed the book.

1.2 A tour of the box

Everything on the panel is numbered in the picture.

  • 1The screen, at the top right. It shows one page at a time, and every page is laid out the same way, which section 1.5 is about.
  • 2The four encoders, two above the screen and two below. They turn forever in either direction, with no end stop, and they push in like buttons as well.
  • 3The function buttons, the grid of buttons under the screen, three across and six down. Each one takes you to a page: on Ember they're called things like LFO, DCO and VCF, on Step ENTRY, TRACKS and PLAY, and so on.
  • 4The keys, down the left-hand side: white keys along the edge, black keys beside them.
  • 5OCT- and OCT+, the two small buttons above the keys. They move the keys down or up; section 1.4 has the details.

Two of the function buttons are the same on every unit, and they're always in the same place:

  • 6SOUNDS, in the middle of the bottom row, where you choose a sound (section 1.9). Step, which has no sounds of its own, keeps its songs on SONG instead, just above SETUP.
  • 7SETUP, at the bottom right, for the settings that aren't part of any sound (section 1.10).

Your buttons, your labels

If your unit has the plain top panel, the words under the buttons are the ones you wrote on the white strip when you built it. This book uses the names each button has in the firmware, the same ones that appear in the top bar of the screen, so if the book says VCF and your strip says something else, the screen will settle it.

1.3 Two ways to hold it

Upright, the way the pictures in this book show it, is for setting things up: the screen's at the top and the encoders fall nicely under your fingers.

Turned a quarter of the way round to the left, a unit becomes a little piano: the lowest note on the left, the white keys nearest you. That's for playing a sound to hear what it's like. The screen doesn't turn round with it, so it'll be on its side, but you won't be reading it much while you play.

In this book you'll mostly leave your units upright, side by side on the desk, and let Step play them. Their keys are for trying a sound out, and Step's keys are for writing notes, which chapter 3 shows you.

1.4 The keys

There are twenty-seven keys: two octaves and a little bit, from C3 at the top (when the unit's upright) to D5 at the bottom. Middle C, C4, is the eighth white key down, just above halfway. They aren't touch-sensitive, so every note plays at the same loudness however hard you press. A MIDI keyboard plugged into the Root fixes that, and section 1.11 says how.

OCT- and OCT+ move the keys down or up:

  • ·Tap one to move the keys an octave, up to three octaves either way. While the keys are moved, the light beside that button is on, so you can always see that you've moved them.
  • ·Hold one, and the KEYBOARD page appears for as long as you hold it: encoder 1 moves the keys by octaves, encoder 2 by single semitones, and the screen shows the lowest and highest notes the keys now play.
  • ·Press both together and the keys go back to where they started.

Moving the keys only changes what your fingers play. It isn't part of the sound, and it doesn't change notes coming from Step or a MIDI keyboard. Strike, the drum unit, has no OCT buttons at all, because its keys are drums rather than notes.

1.5 Pages, and the four corners of the screen

Each function button has its own page. Press VCF on Ember and the VCF page comes up, with the filter's settings on it. Press ENV and you're on the envelope page instead. There's no menu to dig through, and nothing to scroll: one button, one page.

A few buttons have a second page, which you get to by pressing the same button again. Press it once more and you're back on the first. You'll meet these as they come up, and they're always written as a route with the page's name in it, like VECTORVECTOR ENV. Press until the top bar says VECTOR ENV.

Now the most useful thing in this whole chapter. Every page has up to four boxes, one in each corner of the screen, and each box belongs to an encoder. The encoders sit in the same pattern as the boxes: two above the screen, two below.

  • 1Encoder 1, top left, changes the top-left box.
  • 2Encoder 2, top right, changes the top-right box.
  • 3Encoder 3, bottom left, changes the bottom-left box.
  • 4Encoder 4, bottom right, changes the bottom-right box.

That's it. You never have to remember which encoder does what: look at the screen, find the box you want, and turn the encoder in that corner. When you turn one, the name in its box changes colour, so you can see which one you touched last.

Try this

Press any function button. Look at the four boxes, then turn each encoder in turn, a few clicks one way and back again, and watch which box changes. Do it on two or three different pages. After about a minute you'll stop thinking about it, which is the point.

Encoders do three things:

  • ·Turn. Slowly, and each click moves the value by one step. Quickly, and it moves several steps a click, so you can cross a big range in one sweep and then slow down for the last bit.
  • ·Push. On some boxes, pushing the encoder in does a second job: switching something on and off, or moving to the next letter of a name. The book says when.
  • ·Hold. Anything that can't be undone, such as copying over one of your songs or resetting the unit, needs the encoder held in. A bar appears along the bottom of the screen and fills up, and only when it's full does the thing happen.

Changed your mind?

Let go before the bar is full and nothing happens at all. That's what the bar is for.

1.6 The top bar

Along the top of every page there's a dark strip with two things in it.

On the left, the name of the page. It's the same name the button has, and it's the name in the route pills. If you're ever not sure where you are, look here.

On the right, on a synth, where the sound you're playing lives, as a short code: FA01, UB07. The first letter is F for one of the factory sounds or U for one of your own; the second letter is which bank (A, B, C...); the number is which sound in that bank. FA01 is the first factory sound, UB07 is the seventh of your own in your second bank.

A small padlock next to the code means it's a factory sound: you can change it while you play, but nothing you do is ever kept in it. A small star in the padlock's place means the sound has changes that aren't kept anywhere yet. Section 1.9 explains both.

1.7 The lights

Every key and every button has a small red light beside it, and the lights are always telling you something.

  • ·Bright beside a function button: that's the page you're on. Beside a key: that note is playing, whether you pressed it or Step is playing it. Beside OCT- or OCT+: the keys are moved that way.
  • ·Dim and blinking mean different things on different units: on Step, a dim light on a key is a step with a note on it, and a blinking one is the step playing now. Each chapter says what they mean when it matters.
  • ·Off: nothing to say.

When you first turn a unit on, the screen shows its name and the firmware version for a moment. Press anything, or turn anything, and it goes away at once.

If the Root carries newer firmware for the unit than the unit has, the next screen says NEW FIRMWARE, with the old and new version numbers. Hold encoder 4 until the bar fills to update it: your sounds and songs are kept. Or press or turn anything else to carry on as you were; it will ask again the next time the unit is turned on.

1.8 Joining units together

A Tessel is a row of units joined side by side, with the Root at the left-hand end. Each unit takes its power from the one on its left and passes it on, and each one's sound travels back along the row to the Root, which mixes them all together for your headphones. A row of joined units is called the chain.

  • ·Joining: slide a unit up against the right-hand side of the last one, so the edges interlock, and the magnets pull them together. Its screen lights up straight away.
  • ·Parting: slide it away. You can do this whenever you like, with everything playing: nothing is lost, because every unit keeps its own sounds and settings, and when you join it on again it comes back exactly as it was.
  • ·How many: up to eight units on one Root. How many the Root can give power to depends on what powers the Root: a good USB-C charger runs them all.

Each unit on the chain gets a name made of what it is and a number, such as STRIKE 10, VOLT 1 or GLASS 2. The number is its MIDI channel, which is how Step (and a keyboard or a computer) picks which unit it's talking to. Units are given their channels automatically, each its own, and a unit keeps its channel when you take it off and put it back: you don't need to do anything. Strike takes channel 10 by itself, the channel drum machines have used since the 1980s.

The order of the units in the row doesn't matter for anything in this book: Step finds every unit wherever it is.

Try this

Join Step, Strike and Volt to the Root, in any order. Look at each one's screen: SETUP, encoder 1, shows each unit's name and MIDI channel. Now take Volt off and put it back on: it comes back with the same name.

1.9 Choosing sounds

Every synth comes with its own collection of sounds, made at the factory, and room for plenty of your own. They live in banks of up to 32 sounds each: one or more factory banks (FAC A, FAC B...) and four banks of your own (USER A to USER D). Every track in this book starts from the factory sounds, so this is the section you'll use most.

On the SOUNDS page:

  • 1BANK, encoder 1: which bank.
  • 2SOUND, encoder 2: which sound in it. The sound changes the moment you turn it, so you can play a few notes, turn, play again.
  • 3COPY TO, encoder 3: turn it to choose one of your own slots, then hold it in to copy the sound you're playing into that slot.
  • 4NAME, encoder 4: on one of your own sounds, turn it to change a letter of the name, and push it to move on to the next letter.

So choosing a factory sound is always the same route. To choose Volt's DISCO BASS, for instance:

on VOLT, SOUNDS›1BANK›FAC A›2SOUND›DISCO BASS

Two units have quicker ways as well, because they're often changed mid-track:

  • ·Strike, the drums: its six factory kits each have a button of their own, down the left-hand column (BOOM, PUNCH, SPARK, VELVET, NEON and TIMBER), so one press changes the whole kit. USER, at the top of the middle column, goes back to the last of your own kits.
  • ·Haze, the effects: its white keys are sixteen presets, one press each, and a press sends every synth into that effect at once.

Try this

Go through the first factory bank on Volt, playing a few notes on each sound. Don't be careful about it. Find two or three you like and remember their codes from the top bar.

Changing a sound

Turn something on a factory sound and you'll hear it change. Go ahead: in this book you'll often open a filter or lengthen a sound to make it fit a track. But the factory sound itself never changes. The padlock in the top bar turns into a small star, which means "changed, but not kept anywhere". Choose the sound again on the SOUNDS page and it's back as it came: that's your undo.

Your changes go when you choose any other sound, so the first time you turn away from a changed sound the screen says EDITS NOT KEPT and stays where it is: copy it if you want to keep it, or turn again to move on. They do survive turning the unit off.

To keep a change, copy the sound into one of your own slots, SOUNDS›3COPY TO›UA01›hold3. The copy takes your changes with it, and from then on every change you make to it is kept.

Songs remember which sound, not the changes

Step can remember which sound every unit was playing in a song (chapter 5 shows you how), but not changes you haven't kept. If a sound in your song has a star, copy it to one of your own slots first. Step will remind you.

It saves itself

There's no SAVE button anywhere. Every unit, Step included, saves what you've done a moment after you do it. You can take a unit off the chain whenever you like, even halfway through writing a bar, and when you put it back it'll be exactly where you left it.

Your own sounds and songs aren't kept in the unit alone: they're kept on the Root as well, which every unit of the same kind shares. Join a unit to a different Root, a friend's or a new one, and if the sounds aren't the same, the unit asks before anything happens: Making Sounds, section 1.8, has the details.

1.10 SETUP

SETUP, at the bottom right, is where the settings that aren't part of any sound live. It has two parts, and pressing SETUP again (or pushing any encoder) moves on through their pages.

THIS UNIT comes first: the settings that belong to this one unit. Encoder 1 is always the unit's MIDI channel (section 1.8), and the others are that unit's own settings, such as how far pitch bend goes, or how much louder Strike plays a step Step has accented. The last THIS UNIT page is RESET, which puts things back the way they left the factory, turns the unit into another kind of unit (REFLASH), or tests it. Making Sounds, section 1.9, goes through every choice.

EVERYTHING means everything

RESET to EVERYTHING wipes your own sounds, and on Step your songs. There's no getting them back, unless you've made a BACKUP to the Root's memory card first (ROOT, encoder 4, below). If you've got a card, do that first.

ROOT comes after THIS UNIT, and it's the settings of the Root, which has no screen or buttons of its own. Every unit's SETUP can reach them, and they're the same whichever unit you use:

  • ·INPUT and GAIN: which of the Root's inputs units record from (the LINE/MIC socket, or the little microphone built into the Root's top), and how loud. Taste and Grit, the sampling units, have them on their own recording pages too.
  • ·MIDI OUT: what the Root's MIDI OUT sends to a computer or another synth: NOTES (Step's notes, each on the channel of the unit it plays), CLOCK (Step's tempo, with start and stop, so other gear plays in time), BOTH, THRU (a copy of what comes in at MIDI IN), or ALL of them.
  • ·CARD: hold encoder 4 to run a job on the Root's memory card. BACKUP copies every unit on the chain, your songs included, into a new folder on the card, never over an old one. RESTORE puts the newest backup back. FORMAT empties the card.

1.11 Playing from a MIDI keyboard

Plug a MIDI keyboard into the Root's MIDI IN socket ("What you need", at the start of the book, says which keyboards and which cable) and you can play any unit from it: with the pitch bend and mod wheels, a sustain pedal, and notes that can get louder the harder you play.

On the ROOT2 page of SETUP, MIDI IN decides how the Root passes notes on: CHANNELS, where each unit plays only the notes on its own channel (the usual way, with a computer), or FOLLOW, where the Root sends your keyboard's notes to whichever unit you last touched. FOLLOW is the easy way to play several units from one keyboard: turn a knob on the unit you want and play.

1.12 When something seems wrong

  • ·There's no sound. Check the volume on the Root, and that every unit is joined on properly (its screen will be lit). On Step, check the MIXER page: a unit turned down to OFF or muted plays nothing.
  • ·A unit plays the wrong notes, or none. Look at OCT- and OCT+ on it: if one is lit, its keys are moved (Step's notes aren't). Then check which unit Step's track is playing: chapter 3 shows where.
  • ·There's a star in the top bar. The sound has changes that aren't kept anywhere. Copy it to one of your own slots to keep them, or choose the sound again to throw them away (section 1.9).
  • ·You're lost. Look at the top bar. It always says which page you're on.
  • ·The screen says FLASH FULL. The unit's memory is full, almost always of samples or songs. Save what you want to keep to the card, then clear what you don't need on SETUP's RESET page, which lists what's using the space.

That's chapter one, and it's the same on every unit, so you'll only ever need to learn it once. Next, a short history of how we got here: from the first electronic instruments to the music in this book.

Chapter 2 - A short history of electronic music

A hundred years of people plugging things in to see what happens.

Every kind of music in this book grew out of the ones before it, and most of them were invented by people misusing machines built for something else. This chapter draws the line from the first electronic instruments to the dance floor. Each chapter of music then picks up its own part of the story in more detail.

2.1 Instruments from electricity

In 1920 a Russian scientist, Léon Theremin, was working on a device for measuring gases when he noticed that the whine it made changed as his hand moved near it. He turned it into an instrument you play without touching: one hand near an upright aerial for pitch, the other near a loop for loudness. The theremin's eerie, swooping voice became the sound of every 1950s film about flying saucers, and the virtuoso Clara Rockmore showed it could play classical music as beautifully as a violin.

In France, Maurice Martenot built the ondes Martenot in 1928: an electronic instrument with a keyboard and a ring on a wire for sliding between notes. Composers took it seriously from the start. Olivier Messiaen gave it a starring part in his huge Turangalîla-Symphonie, first played in 1949, where its voice floats above a full orchestra, and it's still played in concert halls and on film soundtracks today.

These were new instruments, but they were played like old ones: one note at a time, by hand, from a score. The next idea changed what music could be made of.

2.2 Music from recordings

Pierre Schaeffer, an engineer at French radio, recorded steam trains in 1948 and made a piece of music out of the recordings: the Étude aux chemins de fer. He called this musique concrète, music made from real recorded sounds, cut up, slowed down, reversed and layered, first on records and then on tape. Any sound could now be music.

In Cologne, Karlheinz Stockhausen went the other way and built music from pure electronic tones, then mixed the two in Gesang der Jünglinge (1956), where a boy's singing voice is woven through electronic sound. At the 1958 World's Fair in Brussels, the Philips Pavilion, designed largely by the composer and architect Iannis Xenakis, played music by Edgard Varèse and Xenakis himself from hundreds of loudspeakers spread across its walls, so the sound moved around the audience.

In Britain the same ideas came out of the BBC Radiophonic Workshop, set up in 1958 to make sound effects and music for radio and television. Its most famous piece is the Doctor Who theme of 1963, which Delia Derbyshire built from Ron Grainer's score note by note, out of test-tone oscillators and cut tape, with no synthesiser at all: there weren't any yet.

Meanwhile, at Bell Labs in America, Max Mathews was teaching computers to make sound. In 1961 an IBM computer there sang "Daisy Bell", the first song ever sung by a computer.

2.3 The synthesiser

The synthesiser as we know it arrived in 1964, when Robert Moog in New York and Don Buchla in California each built a modular synthesiser: a cabinet of separate electronic modules, oscillators, filters, envelopes and amplifiers, joined by patch cords, where a voltage could control pitch, brightness or loudness. Making Sounds is about what those modules do; this book is about what people did with them.

Wendy Carlos's Switched-On Bach (1968), Bach played on a Moog one painstaking line at a time, became one of the best-selling classical records ever made. Two years later Moog shrank the modular into a portable keyboard, the Minimoog, and synthesisers began moving from studios onto stages and into bands.

The same modulars had sequencers: rows of knobs, one per step, that played a repeating pattern of notes by themselves. In Germany, Kraftwerk built their whole music around machines repeating patterns, on Autobahn (1974), Trans-Europe Express (1977) and The Man-Machine (1978), and Tangerine Dream built long hypnotic pieces from sequenced loops. In 1977 Giorgio Moroder made Donna Summer's "I Feel Love" with a sequenced Moog bass line pulsing under the whole song: a disco hit that sounded like nothing before it, and one many people point to as the moment dance music became electronic.

Brian Eno's Ambient 1: Music for Airports (1978) was made partly from tape loops of different lengths drifting in and out of time with each other: music meant to be "as ignorable as it is interesting". Chapter 7 does the same thing on Step.

2.4 Drum machines, and new rules

By the late 1970s cheap electronics put rhythm machines into home organs, and then into boxes of their own. Roland's CR-78 (1978) let you write your own patterns, and in 1980 Roland brought out the TR-808. It was meant to sound like a real drummer, for musicians to practise and make demos with, and it didn't: its kick drum was a long electronic boom, its handclap a burst of hiss, its cowbell like nothing on earth. It sold badly. Then, second-hand and cheap, it fell into the hands of people who loved how it sounded. Afrika Bambaataa and the Soulsonic Force's "Planet Rock" (1982), which borrowed a Kraftwerk tune and laid it over an 808, started electro, and the 808's boom has been under hip-hop ever since.

In 1983 the instrument makers agreed on MIDI, a common language for electronic instruments, so one keyboard or sequencer could play any synth or drum machine, whoever made it. It's the same language the Root speaks today. In the same years samplers arrived, which record any sound and play it back from the keys, and by the late 1980s hip-hop producers were building whole records from short slices of old funk and soul records on machines such as the E-mu SP-1200 and the Akai MPC60. Chapter 6 is about that.

2.5 House and techno

In Chicago in the early 1980s, DJs such as Frankie Knuckles at the Warehouse club played disco, soul and European electronic records, and stretched and re-edited them for the dancers. When disco records dried up, local producers made their own on drum machines and cheap synths: Jesse Saunders' "On and On" (1984) is often counted as the first house record, and the music took its name from the Warehouse. The TB-303, Roland's failed bass-line box, was turned into something new there in 1987, when Phuture turned its knobs while it played and made "Acid Tracks". House is chapter 5, and acid chapter 4.

A few hundred miles away in Detroit, three friends from the suburb of Belleville, Juan Atkins, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson, took Kraftwerk's cold, mechanical sound, crossed it with funk and electro, and made techno on the same cheap machines. In 1988 house and acid reached Britain and set off the "Second Summer of Love": warehouse parties, outdoor raves, and a youth movement the newspapers didn't understand. Techno is chapter 3.

2.6 Everything since

British rave music sped up and broke apart. Producers chopped up old funk drum breaks on samplers, played them at twice the speed of the bass, and around 1992-94 that became jungle, and then drum and bass: Goldie's Timeless (1995) took it into the album charts. That's chapter 8. Ambient came back as the "chill-out room" at raves, where acts such as The Orb played slow, drifting music for dancers to rest to.

Through the 2000s computers became powerful enough to be whole studios, and a new generation made music in bedrooms on laptops: dubstep came out of south London, and electronic music became pop music. Then many of those producers went back to hardware for its feel and its sound, and the synthesisers of the 1980s came back too, in synthwave, which is chapter 9.

The thread through all of it

Look back through this chapter and the same thing happens again and again. Someone gets hold of a machine, uses it for something it wasn't meant for, and makes something nobody had heard before: a gas detector that sings, a recording of trains, a practice drum machine, a bass box for guitarists. The machines in this book are made to be used, and misused, in exactly that spirit.

Chapter 3 - Techno

A kick drum on every beat, and the patience to change one thing at a time.

Techno is the simplest music in this book, and one of the hardest to get right. Underneath, a techno track is a kick drum on every beat, a hi-hat between them, a clap, and a bass line a bar or two long, round and round for six minutes. What makes it work is everything around that: which parts play when, how a sound slowly changes, and when to take something away so its coming back hits harder.

That's why it's the first style in the book. You'll learn to write a pattern on Step, to make a short pattern into a long one, and to build a whole track out of a few loops by switching them on and off. Every other chapter uses those three things.

What you need for this chapter

The Root, Step, Strike and Volt, joined in a row, in any order, and headphones. Track 3 can use Haze and Glass as well, but you don't need them.

3.1 Where techno came from

Techno was made in Detroit in the 1980s, by three friends who'd met at school in Belleville, a small town outside the city: Juan Atkins, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson. Detroit was the Motor City, and by then its car factories were closing and its centre was emptying out. The three of them listened to Kraftwerk and to European synth-pop on the radio, to funk and to Parliament, and to the electro coming out of New York, and they wanted to make music that sounded like the future: cold, mechanical and still funky.

Atkins got there first. With Rick Davis, as Cybotron, he made "Alleys of Your Mind" (1981) and "Techno City" (1984), and then, on his own as Model 500, "No UFOs" (1985). He'd taken the word from Alvin Toffler's book The Third Wave, which talked about "techno rebels". Derrick May, as Rhythim Is Rhythim, made "Strings of Life" (1987), all rushing piano chords and strings with no bass line at all, and Kevin Saunderson made "Big Fun" (1988) with Inner City, which went into the pop charts. In 1988 a British record label put their tracks on one album, Techno! The New Dance Sound of Detroit, and the music had its name.

They made it on cheap, second-hand machines: Roland's TR-808 and TR-909 drum machines, a few synths, and a sequencer to play them. The 909's kick, short and hard with a click on the front, became the sound of the music, and still is.

The second wave stripped it down. In Detroit, Underground Resistance, with Jeff Mills and "Mad" Mike Banks, made hard, fast, angry records and kept themselves anonymous, and Robert Hood made Minimal Nation (1994), which kept only what a track couldn't do without. When the Berlin Wall came down in 1989, the city was full of empty buildings, and techno moved in: the Tresor club opened in 1991 in an old department store's vault, and Detroit's producers played there and released records on its label. Berlin has been techno's second home ever since.

Today techno is played all over the world, from small basements to festivals, and it comes in every kind, from the deep and dubby to the fast and harsh. What hasn't changed is the kick drum on every beat, and the idea that a few parts, changed slowly, are enough.

3.2 What techno is made of

Put on a techno record and listen for these. Most tracks have every one.

  • ·The tempo. Somewhere between about 120 and 140 beats a minute, steady from start to end. Track 1 is 130.
  • ·A kick on every beat. Four in a bar, every bar. It's called "four to the floor", and it's the part dancers move to. Everything else fits round it.
  • ·Hi-hats on the off-beats, exactly halfway between the kicks: kick, hat, kick, hat. It's the "tss" in "boom tss boom tss", and it pulls the beat forward.
  • ·A clap or a snare on beats 2 and 4, with the second and fourth kicks. It gives the bar a shape: one, two, three, four.
  • ·A bass line that stays out of the kick's way. The kick and the bass are both low and heavy, and if they play at the same moment they blur into one. So techno bass lines usually rest on the beat and play in the gaps.
  • ·Eight bars at a time. Something changes every eight bars (or sixteen, or thirty-two): a part comes in, a part drops out. Dancers feel it coming even if they've never counted a bar in their lives, and so will you.
  • ·Slow change. A filter opening over a minute, a sound getting longer, a part slowly louder. In music this repetitive, a small change sounds big.

Notice what isn't on that list. Most of the music you know moves through chords: a hymn, a pop song or a symphony sets off from home, goes somewhere else, and comes back, and the pull to get home is a large part of what carries you along. That journey from chord to chord is a chord progression, and it's most of what music theory calls harmony. Techno deliberately throws it out. A track sits on one chord, often on one note, for six minutes, and never goes anywhere in that sense. (Track 1's bass does move, A, F, G, E, but it's a riff going round, not a journey: it never arrives, it just comes round again.) What carries you along instead is the sound itself, changing slowly: parts coming in and dropping out, a filter opening, the same few bars heard a little differently each time round.

That idea didn't start on the dance floor. In the 1960s and 70s a group of American composers, the minimalists, came at it from the concert hall. Terry Riley's In C (1964) is 53 short phrases that players repeat as many times as they like; Steve Reich built whole pieces from one pattern played against itself as it slowly drifts out of step, as in Clapping Music (1972) for two pairs of hands; his Music for 18 Musicians (1976) holds each chord for minutes while the patterns shift over it. Philip Glass worked the same way, and John Adams, who came a little later, carried it into opera and song: his "songplay" I Was Looking at the Ceiling and Then I Saw the Sky (1995) sets young people's lives in Los Angeles around its 1994 earthquake to numbers built on repeating pop, gospel and funk grooves. Repetition, slow change, and the sense that the music is a place you're in rather than a story being told: listen to any of them next to a techno track and you'll hear the family likeness. The two worlds have met, too: the Orb's "Little Fluffy Clouds" (1990) is built on a sample of Reich's Electric Counterpoint.

A word about counting, since the rest of the book does a lot of it. A beat is one kick, one tap of your foot, and beats are grouped into bars. How many beats a bar has is the music's time signature: a waltz counts in threes (3/4), a jig in sixes (6/8), but almost all dance music counts in fours, 4/4, and so does everything in this chapter. In 4/4 each beat is a crotchet. A crotchet splits into two quavers, and a quaver into two semiquavers, so a bar of 4/4 has four crotchets, eight quavers and sixteen semiquavers.

Step's screen writes lengths as fractions, the way sequencers always have: 1/4 is a crotchet, 1/8 a quaver, 1/16 a semiquaver, and 1 a whole bar of 4/4 (a semibreve). The fractions come from the American names, quarter, eighth and sixteenth notes, which you'll meet in plenty of other manuals. Step writes a place in the song as three numbers, 2:4.1: bar 2, beat 4, the first semiquaver of that beat.

3.3 Track 1 at a glance

Here's the first track, all of it, before you build it. Listen to it first, so you know where you're going.

Sound 3.1  Track 1, as built in sections 3.4 to 3.6: four one-bar loops, brought in and out by muting tracks, and Volt's filter opened by hand from bar 41.

It's made of four one-bar patterns, each on its own Step track:

That's all the music there is. Sixty-four bars, about two minutes, are made from those four patterns by switching tracks on and off, eight bars at a time:

Track 1

The whole track, as you'll set it up.

STEPTEMPO 130
STRIKEPUNCH
VOLTPLUCK BASS (FA09)OCT- once
TRACK 1STRIKELOOP 1 BARKICK on every beat
TRACK 2STRIKELOOP 1 BARCL HAT on the off-beats
TRACK 3STRIKELOOP 1 BARCLAP on 2 and 4
TRACK 4VOLTLOOP AUTOA F G E, 2 bars each
MIXERVOLT -6

PUNCH is Strike's hard, bright kit, with a short kick that has a click on the front: just what techno wants. PLUCK BASS is a Volt sound whose filter snaps open and shut on every note, so each one is a short, rubbery pluck: if you've read Making Sounds, it's much like the one you built in its section 4.7.

3.4 Setting up

A new song

If Step has a song in it already, start a new, empty one, so nothing old gets in the way. Your old song isn't touched: it stays in Step's list on the SONG page.

on STEP, SONG›4ACTION›NEW›hold4

The sounds

  • 1On STRIKE, press PUNCH.
  • 2On VOLT, choose PLUCK BASS, SOUNDS›1BANK›FAC A›2SOUND›PLUCK BASS, then press FILTER, ready for later, and OCT- once. PLUCK BASS is a bass, and with its keys an octave down, the key you'll write it with sits where it should.

The tempo

On STEP, TEMPO›1TEMPO›130. A new song starts at 120.

Four tracks

Step has sixteen tracks, and each one plays one unit. You can give several tracks to the same unit, and in techno you usually will, one per drum: then each drum is a part of its own, which you can switch off and on by itself, or make a different length. Track 1 will be the kick, 2 the hats, 3 the clap, all on Strike, and 4 the bass, on Volt.

On the TRACKS page, encoder 1 (TRACK) chooses the track, and encoder 2 (UNIT) chooses which unit it plays, by name:

  • 1On STEP, TRACKS›1TRACK›1›2UNIT›STRIKE. The name has a number after it, its MIDI channel: STRIKE 10.
  • 21TRACK›2›2UNIT›STRIKE, and the same for track 3.
  • 31TRACK›4›2UNIT›VOLT.

Step may have given some tracks a unit already: it gives empty tracks to units on the chain that nothing's playing yet. Turn UNIT anyway, until it says what the list says.

How long each track goes round

The third box on TRACKS, LOOP, says how long a track plays before it goes back to its start. AUTO, the setting a new track has, means "as long as my notes go": the bass will be eight bars long, so on AUTO it plays all eight bars, then starts again. A set number of bars means "go round every this many bars, whatever else is happening". The drums only need one bar each, so:

  • 11TRACK›1›3LOOP›1 BAR
  • 2The same for tracks 2 and 3. Leave track 4 on AUTO.

Now you write each drum's bar once, and it plays for as long as the song does.

3.5 Writing the patterns

Notes are written on Step's ENTRY page. It works like a typewriter: there's a cursor, the place in the song where the next note goes, and every time you play a note it's written there and the cursor moves on.

  • 1LENGTH, encoder 1: how long the next note is, and so how far the cursor moves on: 1/4 is a crotchet (a beat, here), 1/8 a quaver (half a beat), 1/16 a semiquaver (a quarter of a beat). Push it in for a rest: the cursor moves on by that length, leaving a gap.
  • 2PITCH, encoder 2: the note. You won't need it here: the keys choose the note.
  • 3VELO, encoder 3: how hard the note is played. 100 for now; Track 2 uses it.
  • 4BAR, encoder 4: where the cursor is. Turn it to move through the song.

And here's the handy part: you can write with any unit's keys, not only Step's. Press KICK on Strike while Step's ENTRY page is showing track 1, and Step writes a kick. The top bar says which track you're writing and which unit it plays: T1 STRIKE 10.

The kick

  • 1On STEP, TRACKS›1TRACK›1, then ENTRY›1LENGTH›1/4.
  • 2On STRIKE, press KICK four times.

Four kicks, one a beat, and the cursor has moved on to the start of bar 2 (BAR says 2, BEAT 1.1). That's bar 1 done, and with LOOP 1 BAR it'll play in every bar of the song.

The hats

The hats go on the off-beats: a rest the length of a quaver, then a hat, four times over.

  • 1On STEP, TRACKS›1TRACK›2, then ENTRY›4BAR›1.
  • 21LENGTH›1/8.
  • 3Four times: push1 for a rest, then on STRIKE CL HAT.

Back to bar 1 every time

When you change track, the cursor stays where you left it: at the start of bar 2, after the kick. Turn BAR back to 1 before you write the next track (turn it well anticlockwise: it stops at the start of bar 1), or your hats go into bar 2, and with LOOP 1 BAR, bar 2 is never heard.

The clap

  • 1On STEP, TRACKS›1TRACK›3, then ENTRY›4BAR›1›1LENGTH›1/4.
  • 2Twice: push1 for a rest, then on STRIKE CLAP.

The bass

The bass plays semiquavers, three to a beat, and rests on the beat itself, where the kick is. Look back at the bottom row of figure figure 3.1: rest, note, note, note, four times.

  • 1On STEP, TRACKS›1TRACK›4, then ENTRY›4BAR›1›1LENGTH›1/16.
  • 2Four times: push1, then on VOLT A2 three times. With OCT- pressed once, A2 is the sixth white key from the top.

Step's PITCH box says A2. You'll hear it lower, at A1: PLUCK BASS's oscillators are set to sound an octave below the note they're given, as many bass sounds are. Low A is the bottom of a bass guitar, and it's where a techno bass line likes to sit.

Writing from a MIDI keyboard

A MIDI keyboard writes on Step too. On any unit, set SETUP's ROOT 2 page to MIDI IN FOLLOW, turn any encoder on Step so it's the unit you last touched, and play: each note goes in at the cursor, as the keys do, and how hard you played it goes in as its VELO. It's handy for a bass line, where it's quicker to find the notes on a proper keyboard.

One bar of bass into eight

A bass line on one note all the way through would be very minimal techno indeed. Track 1's moves down every two bars, A, F, G, E, then round again: eight bars in all. You could write all eight bars key by key. But it's quicker, and it's how most tracks get built, to copy the bar you've got until there are eight, and then change the notes of the copies. Both are done on the COPY page.

  • 1On STEP, turn 4BAR back one click, so the cursor is inside bar 1 again (just now it's at the start of bar 2). Then press COPY.

COPY opens ready to copy the cursor's bar into the next one. Its boxes say what's copied and where to:

  • ·START and END, encoders 3 and 4, are the stretch to copy: from the start of START's beat to the end of END's beat. So START 1:1.1 and END 1:4.1 are the whole of bar 1, and the line under END counts its notes: 12.
  • ·TO, encoder 2, is where the copy goes: where its first note lands. It starts at the bar just after the cursor's bar, here bar 2 (2:1.1), so the first copy needs no turning. A copy writes over whatever's already at TO, so each time you copy, TO has to move on to the first empty bar after what you've got.
  • ·TO TRACK, encoder 1, is which track the copy goes on: this one, 4, unless you turn it. Leave it on 4.

Encoders 2 to 4 move a beat a click, so four clicks is a bar. Now copy, doubling up: one bar makes two, two make four, four make eight.

  • 2hold4 until the bar fills. Bar 1 is copied into bar 2.
  • 3Now copy bars 1 and 2 into bars 3 and 4. Make the range two bars long, 4END four clicks on to 2:4.1, then move TO past the copy you've just made, 2TO four clicks on to 3:1.1, then hold4.
  • 4And bars 1 to 4 into bars 5 to 8: 4END›4:4.1, then 2TO›5:1.1, then hold4. That's eight bars of A: played now, it sounds just as one bar did, round and round.

New notes for the copies

Now change bars 3 to 8 to F, G and E. That's called transposing: moving notes up or down without changing their rhythm. It's on the COPY page too, because it works on the same kind of stretch of a track, START to END. Push encoder 1 and the page changes job: the top bar says TRANSPOSE T4 instead of COPY T4, and encoder 1's box becomes SEMITONES, how far to move the notes. TO isn't needed, so it shows a dash: the notes stay where they are and only their pitch changes. (Push encoder 1 again for DELETE, which empties the stretch, again for FILL, which repeats it, and once more to come back to COPY. FILL comes into its own in chapter 5.)

F is four semitones below A (A, G#, G, F#, F), so bars 3 and 4 move by -4. G is two below A, and E five below.

  • 5push1 for TRANSPOSE. END is still 4:4.1, so turn 3START›3:1.1: the stretch is now bars 3 and 4. Then 1SEMITONES›-4 and hold4. Bars 3 and 4 are F.
  • 6Bars 5 and 6, to G: 4END›6:4.1 first, then 3START›5:1.1, 1SEMITONES›-2, hold4.
  • 7Bars 7 and 8, to E: 4END›8:4.1, 3START›7:1.1, 1SEMITONES›-5, hold4.

SEMITONES always counts from where the notes are now, and every stretch here is still A, so each one is counted from A.

END first, then START

START can't go past END. When you move the stretch later in the song, move END on first, then START after it: the other way round, START stops where END is.

Press PLAY and listen. Press STOP when you've heard enough. Everything's playing at once, and it already sounds like techno. It just doesn't go anywhere yet.

3.6 Mixing it and playing it

In techno the kick is the loudest thing in the track, and the bass sits just under it. PLUCK BASS is a full, loud sound, so turn Volt down a little on Step's MIXER, which has a box for every unit on the chain:

on STEP, MIXER, then turn the box that says VOLT to =-6

The numbers are decibels (dB), the way sound engineers measure level, and 0 is the unit as it plays. Every 6 dB down halves the signal, but your ears don't hear it that way: they work in ratios, not steps, so -6 sounds clearly quieter, not half as loud. It takes about -10 to sound half as loud, and about -20 to sound a quarter as loud. So small numbers go a long way: 1 or 2 dB is a nudge, 6 is a real change, and 20 puts a part right at the back. Push a box's encoder and that unit is muted, which you won't need here: you'll switch tracks off instead, because that can take one drum out and leave the rest.

Building the track by taking things away

Now the part that makes four loops into a track. On TRACKS, pushing encoder 1 mutes the track it's showing: it stops playing (its notes stay just as they are), the box says MUTED, and pushing again brings it back. You'll play the whole of figure figure 3.2 that way, by hand, while Step plays.

First, mute everything but the kick, so the track starts with the kick on its own:

  • 1On STEP, TRACKS›1TRACK›2›push1, then the same on tracks 3 and 4. Stay on track 4.
  • 2Press PLAY.

While Step plays, the top bar shows a small play arrow and the bar the track you're on has got to. Track 4, the bass, is eight bars long, so on track 4 it counts 1 to 8, then 1 again: each time round is one eight-bar phrase. That's your clock. Every change in this track comes as a new phrase starts, when the 8 turns back into a 1.

PhraseBarsWhat you do as it starts
11-8Nothing: the kick on its own.
29-16Unmute track 2: the hats come in.
317-24Unmute tracks 3 and 4: the clap and the bass.
425-32Nothing: let it play.
533-40Mute track 1. The kick drops out, and everything floats.
6-741-56Unmute track 1, and on Volt, turn CUTOFF up three clicks at the start of every bar, so the bass gets brighter and brighter.
857-64Mute tracks 3 and 4: kick and hats to finish. Press STOP at the end of the phrase.

To make a change, turn TRACK to that track during the last bar of a phrase, and push it as the next one begins. You'll be a little early or late the first time, and it doesn't matter: DJs do this by ear every night, and a part coming in a beat late sounds like you meant it. If you lose count, listen for the bass going back to A: that's a new phrase. Once the bass is muted, keep count in eights in your head, four kicks to a bar.

The filter in phrases 6 and 7 is the one that needs two hands. Volt's FILTER page is already showing, from when you set it up: CUTOFF is encoder 1, and it starts at -2.5. Three clicks a bar for sixteen bars brings it to about +2.3, and you'll hear PLUCK BASS go from a dark thud to a bright, buzzing snarl. Turn slowly: it's more exciting when you can hardly hear it change.

The star on Volt

Once you've turned CUTOFF, Volt's top bar shows a star instead of the padlock: PLUCK BASS is a factory sound, and your change isn't kept in it. That's just what you want here. To play the track again from the start, turn CUTOFF back to -2.5, or choose PLUCK BASS again on SOUNDS.

Try this

Play it again, and this time make your own changes. Take the hats out for the last bar of a phrase and bring them back on the 1. Bring the bass in eight bars later than the plan. Mute the kick for one bar only, just before it comes back. Turn CUTOFF down instead of up. There's no wrong answer: if it makes you want to move, it's right.

That's a techno track: four one-bar loops and the patience to change one thing at a time. Everything's saved as you go, so the song's still on Step when you come back.

3.7 Track 2 at a glance

Track 1 was four loops and the patience to change one thing at a time. Track 2 keeps that, and adds the things that make a drum pattern feel played rather than typed: some notes softer than others, a pattern two bars long instead of one, an open hi-hat, and a bass line that moves. And instead of a slow climb all the way through, it has a breakdown: eight bars where the floor drops away and the tension builds, before everything crashes back in.

Sound 3.2  Track 2, as built in sections 3.8 and 3.9: two-bar hats with an open hat, a bass riff that moves, and soft ghost hats that come in once the groove is settled.

Five tracks this time. The hats come in two kinds: the loud ones on the off-beats, as in Track 1, and soft ghost hats between them.

Track 2

The whole track, as you'll set it up.

STEPTEMPO 132
STRIKEPUNCH
VOLTBOUNCE (FA15)OCT- once
TRACK 1STRIKELOOP 1 BARKICK on every beat
TRACK 2STRIKELOOP 2 BARSCL HAT on the off-beats, OP HAT on the last
TRACK 3STRIKELOOP 1 BARCLAP on 2 and 4
TRACK 4VOLTLOOP AUTOa two-bar riff
TRACK 5STRIKELOOP 1 BARCL HAT, VELO 50, between the off-beats

BOUNCE is a Volt bass with a lot of EMPHASIS, so its filter squelches as it opens, and a little glide, so each note slides into the next instead of jumping: it's what makes the riff bounce. Like PLUCK BASS, it sounds an octave below the note it's given.

3.8 Building Track 2

Most of this is what you did for Track 1, so the routes are shorter. The new parts get the explaining.

A new song

On STEP, SONG›4ACTION›NEW›hold4. Track 1 isn't touched: it's still there on the SONG page, as song 1. To play it again later, SONG›1SONG to it, then push1 to load it.

The sounds and the tempo

  • 1On STRIKE, PUNCH (it may be on PUNCH already).
  • 2On VOLT, SOUNDS›1BANK›FAC A›2SOUND›BOUNCE, then FILTER, ready for the breakdown. OCT- needs to be pressed once, so its light is on: if it's still on from Track 1, leave it alone, as pressing it again would move the keys down another octave.
  • 3On STEP, TEMPO›1TEMPO›132.

Five tracks

On TRACKS, give each track its unit and its loop, as in section 3.4. The new one is track 2: 3LOOP›2 BARS, so it plays two bars before it goes round.

TrackUNITLOOPPlays
1STRIKE1 BARThe kick
2STRIKE2 BARSThe off-beat hats, with an open hat
3STRIKE1 BARThe clap
4VOLTAUTOThe riff, two bars
5STRIKE1 BARThe ghost hats

Tracks of different lengths play side by side without any trouble: the one-bar tracks just go round twice for every time the two-bar ones go round once.

The kick

Exactly as in Track 1 (section 3.5): on track 1, ENTRY›1LENGTH›1/4, then on STRIKE KICK four times. From here on, remember to turn BAR back to 1 each time you change track.

Two bars of hats, and an open hat

Track 2 is Track 1's off-beat hats, but two bars of them, with the very last one an open hi-hat: the long, splashy "tssss" instead of the short "ts". It comes once every two bars, at the end, and it's a little signal to the dancers that the pattern's going round again.

  • 1On STEP, TRACKS›1TRACK›2, then ENTRY›4BAR›1›1LENGTH›1/8.
  • 2Seven times: push1, then on STRIKE CL HAT.
  • 3Then push1 once more, and on STRIKE OP HAT. The cursor is at the start of bar 3: two bars written.

Listen to what the open hat does when it plays: it doesn't ring on for long. The next closed hat cuts it short. On a real drum kit the two are one pair of cymbals, opened and closed by the drummer's foot, so the closed sound always stops the open one, and drum machines have done the same ever since. It's called a choke, and Strike's closed hat always chokes its open hat.

The clap

As in Track 1: TRACKS›1TRACK›3, then ENTRY›4BAR›1›1LENGTH›1/4, and twice push1 and on STRIKE CLAP.

The riff

Track 1's bass sat on one note for two bars at a time. Track 2's moves within the bar: it jumps up an octave and back, steps through C, D and E, and only repeats every two bars. It's still built the same way, though: rest on the beat, where the kick is, and three semiquavers after it.

  • 1On STEP, TRACKS›1TRACK›4, then ENTRY›4BAR›1›1LENGTH›1/16.
  • 2Then, beat by beat, a rest (push1) and three keys on VOLT:
BarBeat 1Beat 2Beat 3Beat 4
1rest, A2, A2, A3rest, A2, C3, A2rest, A2, A2, A3rest, G2, A2, C3
2rest, A2, A2, A3rest, A2, C3, A2rest, E3, D3, C3rest, G2, E2, G2

With OCT- pressed once, Volt's top key is C2, and the white keys go up from there, C D E F G A B, then C again. So, counting white keys from the top: E2 is the 3rd, G2 the 5th, A2 the 6th, C3 the 8th, D3 the 9th, E3 the 10th and A3 the 13th.

A wrong note?

Turn 4BAR back to it and play the right key. Step is in REPLACE (the word under BAR), so the new note goes in where the old one was. Then turn BAR on again to where you'd got to. If it's gone badly wrong, start the track again: TRACKS›hold4 clears every note on it.

The ghost hats

Now the new idea. Every note Step writes has a velocity: how hard it's played, from 1 (as soft as possible) to 127 (as hard as possible). It's called velocity because on a keyboard it's measured by how fast the key goes down. So far every note has been at 100, the VELO box on ENTRY. Turn VELO down before you write, and the notes go in softer: Strike plays them quieter, as a drummer would.

Soft notes between the main ones are called ghost notes, and they're how drummers make a beat feel alive. Track 5's ghost hats go on the second and fourth semiquaver of every beat, in between the off-beat hats.

  • 1On STEP, TRACKS›1TRACK›5, then ENTRY›4BAR›1›1LENGTH›1/16.
  • 23VELO›50.
  • 3Four times: push1, CL HAT, push1, CL HAT.

VELO stays where you left it

VELO doesn't go back to 100 by itself. Whatever you write next, on any track, goes in at 50 until you turn it up again. That's why the ghost hats are written last. When you're done, turn 3VELO›100, or the next thing you write will be mysteriously quiet.

VELO works the same whichever unit's keys you write with: Step's own keys, Strike's, Volt's. Volt plays every note at the same loudness unless its VELO setting is on (Volt's SETUP), so on Volt, velocity makes no difference in this book until chapter 4.

3.9 Playing Track 2

Each song keeps its own mix, so on the new song Volt is back at 0. Turn it down again: MIXER, and the box that says VOLT to -6.

Counting bars the way musicians do

In Track 1, the bass track's counter went 1 to 8, which made it a clock for the phrases. Here the longest track is two bars, so the counter only goes 1, 2, 1, 2. So count the bars the way musicians do: instead of "one, two, three, four" over and over, count the bar number in place of the "one":

ONE two three four, TWO two three four, THREE two three four ... EIGHT two three four

Each word is a kick. When you get to EIGHT, the next bar is a new phrase. It feels clumsy for about a minute and then you'll never lose count again. Once the off-beat hats are in, the open hat helps too: it comes at the end of every second bar, so the fourth open hat ends a phrase.

The arrangement

As in Track 1: on TRACKS, mute every track but the kick (tracks 2, 3, 4 and 5), press PLAY, and make each change as a phrase begins.

PhraseBarsWhat you do as it starts
11-8Nothing: the kick on its own.
29-16Unmute track 2: the off-beat hats.
317-24Unmute track 5: the ghost hats.
4-525-40Unmute tracks 3 and 4: the clap and the riff.
641-48The breakdown. Mute tracks 1 and 2, the kick and the off-beat hats, and on Volt, turn CUTOFF up six clicks at the start of every bar.
749-56Unmute tracks 1 and 2. Everything's back.
857-64Mute tracks 3 and 4: the drums on their own to finish. STOP at the end of the phrase.

The breakdown

Listen carefully to the ghost hats through the track. When they come in at bar 17, they sit comfortably between the off-beat hats and the beat just feels busier. Then in the breakdown the kick and the off-beat hats go, and the ghost hats have nothing left to lean on. Heard on their own, on the second and fourth semiquavers, they sound as if the beat has slipped sideways: your foot isn't quite sure where to go. That's on purpose. Unsettling the listener is half of what a breakdown is for.

At the same time, Volt's filter is opening: CUTOFF starts at -3.0, and six clicks a bar for eight bars takes it to about +1.8. With BOUNCE's high EMPHASIS, the riff squelches and whistles more and more as it opens. Then at bar 49 the kick and the off-beat hats come back, the beat snaps back into place under the ghost hats, and the riff is wide open. That's the drop, and it works because of the eight bars before it.

The same notes, a different meaning

The ghost hats never change in this track: the same eight soft notes every bar. What changes is what's around them. Notes that sound like decoration in one place sound like tension in another. Much of arranging is exactly this: not writing new parts, but changing what each part has around it.

Turn CUTOFF back to -3.0 when you've finished, ready to play the track again (or choose BOUNCE again on SOUNDS).

Try this

Change a note's velocity after it's written: on track 5, turn BAR to a ghost hat and turn VELO, and that note changes. Try making the hats in the second half of each beat a little louder (60) than the first (40), and listen to the groove lean forward. Then turn VELO back to 100.

Move the open hat: on track 2, turn BAR to another off-beat hat and play OP HAT over it. Try the breakdown without the filter, then with the filter but the off-beat hats left in, and hear how much each part of the trick does.

3.10 Track 3: your own

You've built two tracks from recipes. This one is yours. There's no recipe card: there's a list of things you can change, each only a few presses, and you choose. Change one thing or all of them. Section 3.11 shows one way it might go, if you'd like to hear somebody else's choices first, but treat it as the dullest possible answer rather than the right one: there's no right answer, and the best track is the one that makes you want to move.

Start from Track 2

Most tracks start as a copy of another one. Rather than build everything again, copy Track 2's song and change the copy:

  • 1On STEP, make sure Track 2 is the song loaded: SONG›1SONG to it, and push1 if it isn't already.
  • 24ACTION›DUPLICATE›hold4. The copy is the song you're working on now; Track 2 is safe as it was.
  • 3Give it a name, so you can tell them apart: encoder 2, NAME, turns the letter, and pushing it moves on to the next one.

Before you play, check TRACKS: the copy has Track 2's mutes as you left them at the end of playing it. Push encoder 1 on any track that says MUTED and you want to hear.

Choices

  • ·The tempo. On TEMPO. Slower, from about 120 to 126, sounds deeper and more hypnotic, and leaves room for echoes; faster, from 135 to 140, sounds harder and more urgent. A few BPM makes more difference than you'd expect.
  • ·The kit. Press another kit button on Strike while it plays. The patterns stay as they are, because each key is the same drum in every kit: the kick key is always a kick. BOOM has a long, deep, booming kick; SPARK is lighter and thinner. (NEON has drums but no hi-hats or clap, so those tracks go silent: a breakdown of its own.)
  • ·The bass sound. Choose another Volt sound on SOUNDS: PLUCK BASS from Track 1, ROUND BASS, FUNK BASS. The riff stays the same, played by a different instrument.
  • ·The key. Move the whole riff up or down on COPY's TRANSPOSE: START at the start of bar 1, END at the end of bar 2, SEMITONES as you like. Up 5 puts it in D, down 2 in G. If you add a stab (below), do it first, and transpose the stab's track by the same amount, so they stay together.
  • ·The arrangement. Your own order of tracks coming and going, still eight bars at a time. Try starting with something other than the kick, a breakdown twice as long, or a track that never quite settles.

A stab, if you have Glass

A stab is a short chord, played once and left to ring, and it's been in techno since Derrick May's "Strings of Life". You'll need Glass joined to the chain.

  • 1On GLASS, choose a sound: SOUNDS›1BANK›FAC A›2SOUND›E.ORGAN 1. E.PIANO 1 and STRINGS 1, in the same bank, and SYNBRASS 1, in FAC D, all make good stabs too: try each once you've written the chord.
  • 2On STEP, give the stab a track: TRACKS›1TRACK›6›2UNIT›GLASS›3LOOP›1 BAR.
  • 3ENTRY›4BAR›1›1LENGTH›1/8, then push1 three times: the cursor is on the off-beat after beat 2.
  • 4On GLASS, hold down four keys together, A3, C4, E4 and G4, and then let them all go. Step writes them as one chord, and the cursor moves on when the last key comes up.

Look at where those four keys are: A3 is the sixth white key from the top, and the other three are every second white key after it, A, C, E, G, with one white key skipped between each. Stacking notes that way, skipping one each time, is how most chords are built. This one is A minor seventh, made from the same A the riff keeps coming back to, which is why the two sit together so easily.

A stab is loud for its size. On Step's MIXER, turn the box that says GLASS down to about -13, under the drums and the bass.

An echo, if you have Haze

In the early 1990s, two Berlin producers working as Basic Channel slowed techno down and sent its chord stabs into long echoes, borrowed from Jamaican dub, so each chord repeated and faded away behind the beat. It's called dub techno, and it takes two steps on Haze:

  • 1On HAZE, press the sixth white key from the top: the screen says DUB ECHO. An echo that keeps time with Step, and every synth is now sent into it.
  • 2Only the stab should echo, so press SENDS: one box per synth. Turn the boxes that say STRIKE and VOLT to 0, and the one that says GLASS to 60.

Now each stab is followed by its echoes, quieter and quieter, filling the gaps until the next one. Making Sounds, chapter 10, has everything else Haze can do.

3.11 One way it might go

Here's one set of choices: Track 2 duplicated and slowed to 126, the E.ORGAN 1 stab at -13 on the MIXER, and Haze's DUB ECHO on the stab only. Everything else is as Track 2 left it.

PhraseBarsWhat happens
11-8The kick and the stab, and the stab's echoes: before there's any beat to speak of, the echo sets the mood.
29-16The off-beat hats.

Ending as it began is a DJ's favourite: the last eight bars sound like the first eight, so the next record can be mixed in over them.

3.12 What you've learned

Three techno tracks, and along the way most of what Step does day to day:

  • ·Tracks, each playing a unit, several on one unit, each with its own loop: one bar, two bars or AUTO.
  • ·Writing on ENTRY: lengths and rests, BAR, REPLACE, and velocity, from any unit's keys.
  • ·COPY and TRANSPOSE: one bar into eight, and new notes for the copies.
  • ·The MIXER, and arranging by muting and unmuting tracks, eight bars at a time.
  • ·Breakdowns and drops: why taking something away is the strongest move there is.
  • ·New songs, and duplicating one to make another.

Next, acid: the same Step and the same Volt, but the other half of Volt, with accents, slides and a filter that squelches. Your techno tracks are safe on the SONG page whenever you want to come back to them.

Chapter 4 - Acid

One bar of bass, sixteen notes long, and a pair of hands on the knobs.

Acid is techno's closest relative, and it's built in the same way: a kick on every beat, hats between them, a clap on 2 and 4, a bar or two going round and round. The difference is the bass. In acid it isn't a bass line sitting under the beat: it's the lead, a squelching, twisting line of sixteen semiquavers, and the person playing the track spends six minutes turning its knobs while it plays, so it never sounds the same twice.

That sound comes from one machine, and Volt has a half made for it: ACID. This chapter uses it, with two things on Step you haven't met yet, accents and slides.

What you need for this chapter

The Root, Step, Strike and Volt, as for techno, and headphones. Haze is optional, in Track 3. The tracks start from your techno tracks, so read chapter 3 first.

4.1 Where acid came from

In 1981 Roland brought out the TB-303 Bass Line, a small silver box meant to play bass parts for guitarists practising on their own. It had one oscillator, a filter, and a little sequencer you programmed a note at a time, with two odd extras: accent, which made a note louder and brighter, and slide, which made a note glide into the next one. It sounded nothing like a bass guitar, and it was hard to program. Roland stopped making it in 1984, and second-hand ones went for almost nothing.

A few people had already heard something else in it. In 1982 the Indian film musician Charanjit Singh made Synthesizing: Ten Ragas to a Disco Beat, Indian ragas played over a drum machine with a 303 bubbling underneath, years before anyone called it acid; hardly anyone heard it at the time.

In Chicago, three friends who called themselves Phuture, DJ Pierre, Earl "Spanky" Smith and Herb J, bought a second-hand 303 and, not knowing how it was meant to be used, turned its knobs while it played. The result was "Acid Tracks", a twelve-minute track of a 303 line squealing and growling over a drum machine. The DJ Ron Hardy played it at his club, the Music Box, over and over, until the dancers loved it, and when it came out on record in 1987 it gave the music its name: acid house.

A year later acid house reached Britain, and with it the "Second Summer of Love" of 1988: warehouse parties, outdoor raves and the yellow smiley face. Since then the 303's sound has never really gone away. Hardfloor's "Acperience 1" (1992) layered several 303s into one long, building track; Josh Wink's "Higher State of Consciousness" (1995) took a single screaming line into the pop charts; and acid techno, harder and faster, came out of London's squat parties. Today there are more machines that copy the 303 than there ever were 303s.

4.2 What acid is made of

  • ·The line. One bar of semiquavers, sixteen steps, some of them rests. It jumps octaves and repeats, and it's catchy in a way a melody isn't: it's more like a riff that talks.
  • ·Accents. A few notes in each bar are accented: louder, and the filter opens wider and snaps back faster, so they bark. Accents in a row build on each other, so a run of them squeals.
  • ·Slides. A slid note glides into the next one instead of starting it fresh, a little smear of pitch. Sliding down an octave is the classic acid sound.
  • ·The filter, and its resonance. The line's notes barely change, but its sound changes all the time, because the filter is being opened and closed, and its resonance turned up until it whistles.
  • ·Hands on the knobs. This is the big one. An acid track is played, not just written: the knobs are turned slowly through the whole track, and that's where the music is.

Acid is techno's idea pushed even further. In techno, you'll remember (section 3.2), there's no chord progression: the music doesn't travel from chord to chord, it stays put and the sound changes. In acid even the notes barely change. The same bar of line goes round for six minutes, and everything you hear happening is the filter, the resonance and the accents, under someone's hands. It's as close as dance music comes to the minimalists' slow-changing patterns, and Track 2 borrows one of Steve Reich's favourite tricks, a pattern going round against another of a different length.

4.3 Track 1 at a glance

Acid Track 1 is techno Track 1's drums with a new bass: Volt's ACID half, playing a one-bar line with four accents and four slides, and played by turning four of its knobs, one stretch of the track at a time.

Sound 4.1  Acid Track 1: one bar of Volt's ACID half with accents and slides, over techno Track 1's drums on BOOM, played by turning its knobs.

Acid Track 1

Techno Track 1, duplicated, with:

TRACK 4VOLTLOOP AUTOthe line, one bar
