BOOM is Strike's deep, round kit, with a long kick that booms: the other sound of early dance music, alongside PUNCH's harder one. Acid house was made on both.

4.4 Setting up

Techno Track 1, copied

  • 1On STEP, load techno Track 1: SONG›1SONG to it (song 1, unless you've moved things about), then push1.
  • 24ACTION›DUPLICATE›hold4. Then name the copy, on encoder 2, so you can find it again.
  • 3TEMPO›1TEMPO›122. Acid house is a little slower than techno.
  • 4On TRACKS, check each track: push encoder 1 on any that says MUTED, so all four play.

The sounds

  • 1On STRIKE, press BOOM.
  • 2On VOLT, SOUNDS›1BANK›FAC B›2SOUND›ACID. FAC B is Volt's bank of ACID sounds, and the ACID button lights. Leave OCT- as it was for techno, pressed once.
  • 3Press ACID, for the ACID page: TUNING, CUTOFF, RESONANCE and ENV MOD. These four are the instrument you'll play.
  • 4On STEP, MIXER, and turn the box that says VOLT down from -6 to -9: in acid the line squeals, and the kit needs a little more room than in techno.

A clean track for the line

Track 4 still has techno Track 1's bass in it. Clear it: TRACKS›1TRACK›4›hold4, until the bar fills and the screen says TRACK CLEARED. The track keeps its unit, Volt, and its loop, AUTO: only the notes go. (Clearing the copy doesn't touch techno Track 1 itself, which is a separate song.)

4.5 Writing the line

The old bass machines were programmed in passes: first the notes, then which of them were accented and slid. That's a good way to do it on Step too. It splits one hard job into two easy ones, and you get to hear the line on its own before you dress it up.

First, the notes

  • 1On STEP, ENTRY›4BAR›1›1LENGTH›1/16.
  • 2Then, beat by beat, on VOLT (a rest is push1 on Step):
Beat 1Beat 2Beat 3Beat 4
A2, A2, A3, A2rest, C3, A2, G2A2, rest, E3, D3C3, A2, A3, G3

The same keys as techno Track 2's riff, with one new one, G3: the 12th white key from the top. Unlike techno's bass lines, this one plays on the beat as well, right on top of the kick. A 303 line doesn't stay out of the kick's way: it fights with it, and that's half its energy.

Press PLAY and listen to it plain, then STOP.

Then, the accents and slides

On Step, ACCENT and SLIDE are the fourth and fifth buttons down the left-hand column. Press one and it changes the note under the cursor, on or off; the light beside it shows whether the note under the cursor has it. So walk the cursor back through the line with BAR, one semiquaver a click, and press them where the line needs them.

  • 1Turn 4BAR all the way back to 1. The cursor is on the first note.
  • 2Then, a click of BAR at a time, press ACCENT on four notes and SLIDE on four:
StepNotePress
1A2ACCENT
3A3SLIDE: it glides down the octave to the A2 after it
6C3ACCENT
7A2SLIDE: down to G2
9A2ACCENT
11E3SLIDE: down to D3
13C3ACCENT
15A3SLIDE: down to G3

A slide belongs to the note it glides from: the A3 on step 3 is held on, and its pitch slides down into step 4's A2, which doesn't start again. Play it now and listen for the difference: the accents bark, the slides smear, and the line suddenly sounds like acid.

VELO doesn't make accents

On Volt's ACID half, a note is accented only by ACCENT, the way bass machines of this kind have always worked, however high or low VELO is. (From a MIDI keyboard, a note played hard, velocity 100 or more, is accented instead.) On other units, ACCENT just plays a note a little harder.

4.6 Playing Track 1

Volt's ACID page has the four knobs you'll play. Each turns in tenths, a click at a time.

  • 1TUNING: the pitch. Leave it at 5.0.
  • 2CUTOFF: how open the filter is. Low is dark and muffled, high is bright and buzzing.
  • 3RESONANCE: how much the filter rings at its cutoff. Up high, the line whistles and squeals.
  • 4ENV MOD: how far each note opens the filter and snaps it back. Up high, every note goes "yow".

Turn CUTOFF down to 2.0 before you start, so the line begins dark. Then, on TRACKS, mute tracks 2 and 3, the hats and the clap, and press PLAY. Count the phrases as in techno Track 1 (with only one bar in the song, count the bars in your head: ONE two three four, TWO two three four...).

PhraseBarsOn Step, as it startsOn Volt, every bar
11-8Nothing: the kick and the line.Nothing yet: let it sit dark.
29-16Unmute track 2: the hats.
3-417-32Unmute track 3: the clap.CUTOFF up 3 clicks, to about 6.8.
533-40Mute track 1: no kick.RESONANCE up 2 clicks, to about 9.1.
6-741-56Unmute track 1.ENV MOD up 2 clicks, to about 9.7.
857-64Mute tracks 2 and 3: kick and line. STOP at the end of the phrase.CUTOFF down 5 clicks, closing it to about 2.8.

Step on one side, Volt on the other, a hand on each: that's how acid has always been played. Keep the knob moves small and steady. A click or two a bar sounds like nothing while you're doing it, but over sixteen bars the line becomes a different animal, and the listener can't say when it happened.

The star on Volt

Every knob you've turned is a change to the factory ACID sound, so Volt's top bar shows a star: nothing's kept. To play the track again from the start, choose ACID again on SOUNDS, and turn CUTOFF down to 2.0.

Try this

Play it again and follow your ears instead of the table. Push RESONANCE right up with CUTOFF low, then sweep CUTOFF slowly: the squeal moves up through the line. Try ACID 2, Volt's second ACID page (press ACID again): DECAY makes each note's "yow" longer or shorter, and ACCENT how hard the accents bark. Then move the accents: walk BAR through the line and press ACCENT on different notes. Three accents in a row squeal; one on its own barks.

4.7 Track 2 at a glance

Acid Track 2 starts from techno Track 2, with its fuller kit: two-bar hats with the open hat, the clap and the ghost hats. Its line is new, and it does something no line in this book has done yet: it's three beats long, in a bar of four.

Sound 4.2  Acid Track 2, as built in sections 4.8 to 4.10: a three-beat line on Volt's square wave going round against techno Track 2's drums, with an accented kick and a snare holding every bar's first beat.

Follow the line down figure figure 4.4. It starts with the kick, on beat 1 of bar 1. Three beats later it starts again, on beat 4; then on beat 3 of bar 2, then on beat 2 of bar 3: a beat earlier every bar. Only at bar 4 does it start on beat 1 again: four times round the line is three times round the bar, twelve beats either way. In between, its accents land somewhere new every bar, and the line seems to tumble over the beat without ever falling. Playing a pattern of three against a beat of four like this is a polyrhythm, and acid producers have loved it from the start: one short loop makes a line that takes three bars to repeat.

4.8 Setting up

Techno Track 2, copied

  • 1On STEP, load techno Track 2: SONG›1SONG to it, then push1.
  • 24ACTION›DUPLICATE›hold4, and name the copy on encoder 2.
  • 3Leave the tempo at 132. Acid that leans towards techno runs faster than acid house.
  • 4On TRACKS, push encoder 1 on any track that says MUTED, so all five play.

The sounds

  • 1Strike stays on PUNCH, as in techno Track 2: hard, bright, and made for this.
  • 2On VOLT, SOUNDS›1BANK›FAC B›2SOUND›SQ SQUELCH, then ACID for the ACID page.

SQ SQUELCH plays a square wave where ACID played a sawtooth. A sawtooth has every harmonic, so it buzzes; a square has only every other one, the odd ones, and it sounds hollower and woodier, like a clarinet next to a trumpet. Bass machines of this kind had a switch for just these two, and so does Volt: WAVEFORM, on the ACID 2 page.

Making room for the kit

On STEP, MIXER. Turn STRIKE down 4, to -4, and VOLT down from -6 to -19. That's a long way down, and the reason is the line itself. A loop of three beats is so insistent that if it's as loud as the drums, your ear follows it instead of them, and the kick seems to be the thing that's out of step. Whatever is loudest and repeats most strongly is what a listener hears as the beat, so the beat has to be the loudest thing here. (STRIKE comes down too because of what you'll do to the kick in a moment: it gets louder.)

A three-beat loop for the line

  • 1Clear track 4, as in Track 1: TRACKS›1TRACK›4›hold4, until it says TRACK CLEARED.
  • 2Push encoder 3, LOOP. Its title now says LOOP BEATS: it turns a beat a click instead of a bar.
  • 3Turn it 3 clicks, to 0+3: no bars and three beats.

A loop like this runs on its own: from PLAY it goes round every three beats, whatever the drums are doing, and Step never starts it again with the song. (When you turn to another track, LOOP counts in bars again.)

4.9 Writing the line, and holding the bar

The line

Notes first, then accents and slides, as in Track 1. On STEP, ENTRY›4BAR›1›1LENGTH›1/16, then on VOLT (a rest is push1 on Step):

Beat 1Beat 2Beat 3
A2, A2, A3, A2rest, C3, D3, E3A2, G2, A3, A2

Twelve semiquavers, and the cursor stops at the end of the loop. VELO still says 50, left from the ghost hats. Leave it: on ACID it makes no difference, as you saw in Track 1.

Then 4BAR back to 1, and through the line a click at a time:

StepNotePress
1A2ACCENT
3A3SLIDE: down the octave to A2
6C3ACCENT
7D3SLIDE: up to E3
10G2ACCENT
11A3SLIDE: down the octave to A2

Three accents, one a beat, each a semiquaver later than the last: on the beat, just after it, then later again. That's what makes the line feel as if it's leaning forward.

Holding the bar

Against a line like this, the drums need to say clearly where each bar starts, its first beat, the "one". Two small things do it.

  • 1An accent on the kick. TRACKS›1TRACK›1, then ENTRY›4BAR›1: the cursor is on the first kick. Press ACCENT. On Strike, an accent plays a drum 6 dB harder (SETUP sets how much), so every bar's first kick now hits harder than the other three.
  • 2A snare with it. TRACKS›1TRACK›6, 2UNIT›STRIKE, and LOOP one click, to 1 BAR. Then ENTRY›4BAR›1›3VELO›100›1LENGTH›1/4, and on STRIKE, press SNARE once.

A snare on beat 1 is an odd place for one: in most dance music it's on 2 and 4, where the clap is here. But on its own, once a bar, it isn't a backbeat. It's a marker, and with the accented kick it plants a flag on the one. The line can tumble as much as it likes; you always know where you are.

4.10 Playing Track 2

This time you'll also play a knob on Volt's second ACID page. Press ACID again for ACID 2: DECAY, ACCENT, WAVEFORM and VOLUME. DECAY is how quickly each note's filter closes after it opens: short is a tight, plucky blip; long lets each note bloom and run into the next. Press ACID again to go back to the first page.

Turn CUTOFF down to 2.0 before you start. On TRACKS, mute tracks 2, 3 and 5: the hats, the clap and the ghost hats. Then press PLAY: the kick, the snare and the line.

PhraseBarsOn Step, as it startsOn Volt, every bar
11-8Nothing: kick, snare and line.Nothing yet.
29-16Unmute track 2: the hats.
3-417-32Unmute tracks 3 and 5: the clap and the ghost hats.CUTOFF up 3 clicks, to about 6.8.
533-40Mute tracks 1, 2 and 6: no kick, no hats, no snare.Press ACID for ACID 2. DECAY up 5 clicks, to about 7.5.

857-64Mute tracks 2, 3 and 5: kick, snare and line. STOP at the end of the phrase.CUTOFF down 5 clicks, to about 2.8.

Listen to the breakdown. With the kick and the snare gone, nothing says where the one is any more: the ghost hats, which unsettled the beat in techno Track 2, and the clap, now don't know where they stand either, and the three-beat line takes over. Everything floats. Then at bar 41 the kick and the snare land on the one together and the whole track snaps back into four.

Counting the phrases is harder this time, because the line keeps pulling you off the bar. Count with the kick, not the line: the accented kick is ONE, every bar.

Try this

Mute track 6 and turn STRIKE and VOLT back to where techno Track 2 had them, 0 and -6, and listen to the line drag the drums into three. Then try other loop lengths on track 4: five beats (LOOP 1+1) comes round every five bars; seven beats every seven. Change WAVEFORM on ACID 2 from the square to the sawtooth while it plays. And move the accents: one in every three semiquavers makes a second, faster three on top of the first.

4.11 Track 3: your own

As in techno, the third track is yours: a copy of Track 2, and a list of things to change. Section 4.12 has one way it might go; the moment yours stops sounding like it, you're doing it right.

Start from Track 2

  • 1On STEP, load acid Track 2: SONG›1SONG to it, and push1.
  • 24ACTION›DUPLICATE›hold4, and name the copy.
  • 3On TRACKS, unmute any track you want to hear.

Choices

  • ·The tempo. Acid house sits around 120 to 125; acid techno, which grew up harder and faster in the 1990s, from about 135 to 145.
  • ·The sound. FAC B has sixteen ACID sounds, each a different starting point for the same knobs: DEEP ACID is darker and rounder, BITE snappier, WAH has a long, vocal sweep, and RUBBER and MELLOW SQ are square waves like SQ SQUELCH.
  • ·The wave. On ACID 2, WAVEFORM swaps the square for the sawtooth and back. The sawtooth is brighter and buzzier, and it's the one that takes distortion best.
  • ·The kit. BOOM for acid house's deeper kick, PUNCH for acid techno's harder one.
  • ·The line. Change a note or two, move the accents and slides, or try another LOOP length: four beats for a straight line, five or seven for a stranger one. Or go back to Track 1's line, sixteen semiquavers, and see how much calmer it sounds over this kit.
  • ·The key. COPY's TRANSPOSE on track 4, START at the start of bar 1, END at the end of beat 3: up 5 puts the line in D.

Distortion, if you have Haze

A 303 line pushed through distortion stops squelching and starts snarling, and acid techno has used it that way ever since. Haze does it in its COLOUR half: the effects it puts on one synth only, the one chosen on its SOURCE page. Join Haze to the chain, then:

  • 1On HAZE, press the 13th white key from the top: the screen says ACID DRIVE. Distortion, a little echo and a little reverb, and every synth is sent into the echo and reverb.
  • 2The drums should stay dry, so SENDS and turn the box that says STRIKE to 0. Leave VOLT's as it is.
  • 3SOURCE. Turn encoder 1, SYNTH, a click at a time until it says VOLT: the one synth whose sound Haze changes.
  • 4Turn encoder 2, MIX, all the way down to 0%. MIX is how much of Volt's sound goes through the distortion: at 0% none of it, at 99% all of it. You'll play it.

MIX is the knob to play here. Turn it up slowly and the distortion creeps in under the clean line until it's all there is. For other kinds of dirt, try Haze's other drive presets, WARM DRIVE (gentler) and FUZZ BASS (fuzzier), or the DRIVE page, where DRIVE sets how hard the sound is pushed.

4.12 One way it might go

Here's one set of choices: acid techno. Track 2 duplicated and sped up to 138, WAVEFORM back to the sawtooth, and Haze's ACID DRIVE on Volt, with MIX at 0% to start. Everything else is as Track 2 left it, the knob moves too, except one: the breakdown is played on Haze instead of on DECAY.

Sound 4.3  Acid Track 3, one way it might go: Track 2 duplicated, at 138 with the sawtooth, and Haze's ACID DRIVE on Volt, played up through the breakdown.

PhraseBarsWhat happens
1-21-16Kick, snare and line, clean, then the hats.
3-417-32The clap and the ghost hats, and Volt's CUTOFF opening, 3 clicks a bar.
533-40The breakdown. Mute tracks 1, 2 and 6, then a hand on Haze: MIX up 12 clicks a bar, to about 96%. The line turns from squelch to snarl with nothing else to hide behind.
6-741-56Everything back, the line now fully distorted, and Volt's ENV MOD up a click a bar.

Notice what the breakdown does this time. In Track 2 it took the kick away and let the line float; here it takes the kick away and changes the line while nobody's looking, so when the kick comes back the track is a harder thing than the one that left. A breakdown doesn't only let the listener breathe: it's the best place in a track to change something for good.

4.13 What you've learned

  • ·Writing in passes, notes first and then accents and slides, as on the old bass machines; ACCENT and SLIDE, and why a slide belongs to the note it glides from.
  • ·Volt's ACID half, and playing a track on its knobs: CUTOFF, RESONANCE, ENV MOD, DECAY.
  • ·Clearing a track, and loops shorter than a bar: three against four, and a line that takes three bars to repeat.
  • ·Balance: the loudest, most insistent part is what the listener hears as the beat, so the beat has to win. Accenting a drum, and marking the one.
  • ·Distortion on one synth with Haze's COLOUR half, played in with MIX.

Next, house: the same four to the floor, but with chords, and whole songs built from sections.

Chapter 5 - House

The same four to the floor, with chords, a shuffle and a bass line that dances.

House is techno's older cousin, from Chicago rather than Detroit, and it's built on the same floor: a kick on every beat, eight bars at a time. But where techno is cold and mechanical, house is warm. It came out of disco and soul, and it kept their chords, their swing and their joy. This chapter brings in the things that make that warmth on Step: chords, and swing.

What you need for this chapter

The Root, Step, Strike, Volt and Ember, and headphones. If you have Glass and not Ember, Glass can play the chords: try E.PIANO 1. Haze comes in later in the chapter.

5.1 Where house came from

In 1977 a New York DJ, Frankie Knuckles, moved to Chicago to play at a new club, the Warehouse. He played disco, soul and gospel records, and European electronic music, and he re-edited them on tape so the best parts lasted longer, the drums were harder, and the dancing never stopped. In New York his old friend Larry Levan was doing the same at the Paradise Garage. When disco fell out of fashion around 1980 and the records dried up, Chicago's DJs and their fans started making their own, on cheap drum machines and synths, and the records were sold as the music they played at the Warehouse: house.

Jesse Saunders' "On and On" (1984) is often counted as the first house record. Two small Chicago labels, Trax and DJ International, put out dozens more, made quickly and pressed cheaply. Ron Hardy played them at the Music Box, rawer and wilder than the Warehouse. Marshall Jefferson's "Move Your Body" (1986), with its piano, called itself "The House Music Anthem", and it was; Larry Heard, as Mr. Fingers, made "Can You Feel It" (1986), soft chords floating over a drum machine, and started deep house. In January 1987 Steve "Silk" Hurley's "Jack Your Body" went to number one in Britain, and house went round the world.

It has never stopped since. Every few years it changes its clothes, garage, deep house, French house, tech house, and comes back. The Daft Punk and Stardust records of the late 1990s ("Music Sounds Better With You", 1998) are house, and so is a good part of what plays in clubs and shops today.

5.2 What house is made of

  • ·The tempo. A little slower than techno: about 118 to 128. Track 1 is 122.
  • ·Four to the floor, as in techno, and a clap or snare on 2 and 4.
  • ·Open hi-hats on the off-beats, the "tss" that rings, where techno usually has a closed one that ticks.
  • ·Swing. A slight shuffle, which comes from disco's and soul's drummers, who never played quite in a straight line.
  • ·A bass line that moves: often on the off-beats, jumping octaves, as in disco.
  • ·Chords. This is the big difference.

In section 3.2 you saw that techno throws out the chord progression: it sits on one chord, or one note, and keeps you moving with slowly changing sound instead. House brings the chords back, from the gospel, soul and disco it grew out of, and they're rich ones: sevenths, chords of four notes, warm and a little bittersweet. But listen to what it does with them. Most house tracks use two chords, or four, round and round, never going on a journey the way a song's verse and chorus do. It's halfway between the two worlds: the harmony of soul music, held in techno's loop. Those chords colour the loop rather than going anywhere, and that's why a house track can last eight minutes and still feel like it's arriving.

5.3 Track 1 at a glance

House Track 1 is two bars long: two chords, a bar each, over a kit with open hats, a bass on the off-beats and a little swing.

5.4 Setting up

A new song, and the sounds

  • 1Join Ember to the chain, on the right of Volt.
  • 2On STEP, SONG›4ACTION›NEW›hold4, and name it.
  • 3On STRIKE, PUNCH.
  • 4On VOLT, SOUNDS›1BANK›FAC A›2SOUND›DISCO BASS, and press OCT- once.
  • 5On EMBER, SOUNDS›1BANK›FAC A›2SOUND›CHORD STAB, then press VCF, ready for later.

DISCO BASS is one of the most famous sounds of its kind of synth, the bubbling, plucked bass of late-1970s disco, and house took it over with the rest of disco's furniture.

Tempo, and swing

  • 1On STEP, TEMPO›1TEMPO›122.
  • 2Turn encoder 3, SWING, up 8 clicks, to 58%. Underneath, it says 1/16: it swings semiquavers.

Played straight, every semiquaver is exactly as long as the next. Swing makes them uneven, in pairs: the first of each pair a little longer, the second a little later. At 58% the first takes 58% of the pair's time instead of half of it, and the second comes in that much late. At 66%, two-thirds, the pair becomes a triplet with its middle note missing, the lilting "shuffle" of blues and jazz. House sits much nearer straight: just enough to make the beat lean back and walk.

Notice which notes move: only the second of each pair, the second and fourth semiquaver of each beat. A note on the beat, or on the off-beat halfway between, never moves at all. So swing does nothing to a part that doesn't play on those semiquavers, which is why this track will put something there for it to swing.

Six tracks

On TRACKS, give each track its unit with encoder 2: tracks 1, 2, 3 and 6 STRIKE, track 4 VOLT, track 5 EMBER. Then LOOP 1 BAR for tracks 1, 2, 3 and 6, the drums; leave 4 and 5 on AUTO.

5.5 The groove

The drums

On STEP, ENTRY, then, a track at a time, from bar 1 (BAR back to 1 each time), on STRIKE:

TrackLENGTHWrite
11/4KICK four times
21/8rest, OP HAT, four times over: the open hats on the off-beats
31/4rest, CLAP, twice

The bass

  • 1Track 4, LENGTH 1/8, on VOLT: rest, A2, rest, A2, rest, A2, rest, A3. The off-beats again, with the hats, and the octave jump at the end of the bar.
  • 24BAR back one, into bar 1, then COPY›hold4: bar 1 is copied to bar 2.
  • 3Push encoder 1 for TRANSPOSE. Turn END on 4 beats, then START on 4, so the range is bar 2 alone, then SEMITONES to +5, and hold4. Bar 2 is now on D.

Up five semitones from A is D: up a fourth, as musicians say, because D is the fourth note counting up from A in A's scale (A, B, C, D). A bass line that steps up a fourth and back is one of the oldest moves in music, and you'll hear why when the chords arrive: they make the same move.

The swung hats

Track 6 is the part the swing works on. On TRACKS, turn to track 6 (it's STRIKE, LOOP 1 BAR), then on ENTRY, BAR to 1, VELO down to 70, LENGTH 1/16, and on STRIKE, four times over: rest, CL HAT, rest, CL HAT.

Soft closed hats on the second and fourth semiquaver of every beat: exactly where the swing moves notes. And each one does something else as well. A closed hi-hat stops an open one, as the real thing does, so the closed hat just after each open hat cuts it short: the open hat's "tssss" becomes a tight "tss-t". It's the house hi-hat sound, made of two parts that fit together.

5.6 The chords

There are two ways to write a chord on Step, and you've already met the first.

By hand. With track 5 open on ENTRY, hold down a chord on Ember's keys and let them all go: Step writes the notes as one chord, as Glass's stab did in techno Track 3. That's the way when you're finding chords by ear.

By name, on the CHORD page. Choose a chord by its name, A minor 7, and Step works out the notes. That's the way when you know what you want, and it's how this track's chords are written.

  • 1On TRACKS, turn to track 5. Then press CHORD: the button under ENTRY.
  • 2Press Step's OCT- once. The CHORD page starts its chords at C4, which is high for chords like these; OCT- moves them down an octave.
  • 34BAR›1›3LENGTH›1/16.
  • 4Turn encoder 1, ROOT, to A. Push it, and encoder 1 turns the TYPE instead (the one underlined is the one it turns): turn it to m7. The screen says Am7, with its four notes under it: A3, C4, E4, G4.

Every time you turn ROOT or TYPE, Ember plays the chord, so you can hear what you're choosing. m7 is a minor seventh, the chord of techno Track 3's stab, built the same way: A, then every other note up from it, A, C, E, G.

The rhythm

Pushing encoder 4 places the chord at the cursor, and the cursor moves on a semiquaver. Turning encoder 4 moves the cursor without placing anything. Place six chords in bar 1, on these semiquavers:

Semiquaver14791215
Dopush4turn 2, push4turn 2, push4turn 1, push4turn 2, push4turn 2, push4

Count it: three semiquavers, three, then two, and the same again. That 3+3+2 is one of the most travelled rhythms in the world. In Cuban music it's called the tresillo, and you'll hear it under salsa, reggaeton, rock and roll and a good share of pop. Against the straight four of the kick it pulls the bar sideways, which is exactly what the chords should do.

The second chord

  • 1Turn encoder 4 on once more, to the start of bar 2.
  • 2Push encoder 1, back to ROOT, and turn it to D: Dm7, D3, F3, A3, C4.
  • 3Turn encoder 2, INVERT, to 2ND: A3, C4, D4, F4.
  • 4Place the same rhythm in bar 2.

INVERT turns a chord over: the lowest note moves up an octave, once for the first inversion, twice for the second. The notes are still D, F, A and C, so it's still D minor 7, but look at them next to Am7's: A3 and C4 are in both, and the other two each move down one step, E to D and G to F. Moving from chord to chord as little as possible, each note taking the shortest way, is what musicians call good voice leading, and it's why the two chords seem to melt into each other instead of jumping. Turn INVERT back to ROOT (not turned over) and listen to the difference: the whole chord drops, and it sounds clumsier.

And the bass: A in bar 1, D in bar 2, the same move up a fourth as the chords. The bass plays each chord's root, the note it's named after, and that's what holds a chord down.

5.7 Balance, and remembering the sounds

On STEP, MIXER. Leave VOLT at 0, level with the drums: house is a dance music, and its bass is half of the dancing. Turn EMBER down to -18. Chords take up a lot of room, four notes at once across the middle of the sound, and a little goes a long way; they're the colour, not the beat.

Then one more thing. This song uses a kit, a bass sound and a chord sound, and next time you load it you want them all back. On STEP, SONG›4ACTION›REMEMBER SOUNDS›hold4. Step asks every unit which sound it's playing, and keeps the answers with the song: whenever you load it again, or press PLAY from the start, every unit goes back to its sound.

Remember before you play

REMEMBER SOUNDS keeps the sound you chose, not changes you've made to it while playing. You're about to turn Ember's filter by hand, which puts a star in its top bar, so remember the sounds first, while everything is as chosen.

On TRACKS, mute tracks 3, 4, 5 and 6, so only the kick and the open hats play, and press PLAY.

Some will sound wrong, some just different; your ears are the judge.

5.11 Four chords

Where chord progressions come from

You don't have to invent a chord progression to use one. Musicians have always borrowed them: a progression isn't owned by anybody, and the same few have carried thousands of songs. Search for something like deep house chord progressions and you'll find lists of them, written as chord names you can dial straight into the CHORD page. That's a fine way to start.

You'll often find them written in Roman numerals instead, like this track's: i, VI, iv, v. The numerals count up the scale from the key's home note. In A minor the scale is A, B, C, D, E, F, G, so A is i, D is iv, E is v and F is VI, a capital numeral for a major chord, a small one for a minor. The point of writing them that way is that the same list works in any key: start on D instead, count up D's scale, and you have the same progression, higher. Lists of progressions are a way in, and every bit of theory you pick up along the way, why one chord leads to another, why some sound sad and some hopeful, makes you freer. More theory is only ever a good thing.

Just don't let it tell you what you're not allowed to do. The Beatles' "Because" (1969), Led Zeppelin's "The Crunge" (1973) and Madness's "Our House" (1982) all go places, harmonically (and in "The Crunge" rhythmically too), that would make a less imaginative composer tut and shake their head, and they're all the better for it. Theory describes what people have found works; it doesn't forbid anything. If it sounds good, it is good.

Writing them

On STEP, on TRACKS turn to track 5, then press CHORD. 4BAR›1; LENGTH is still 1/16 from Track 1, and Step's OCT- still pressed (if its light is off, press it once). Then, for each bar, set the chord and place it in Track 1's rhythm: push encoder 4, then turn 2, push, turn 2, push, turn 1, push, turn 2, push, turn 2, push, and turn on once more to the next bar. Remember that encoder 1 turns whichever of ROOT and TYPE is underlined, and a push swaps them.

BarROOTTYPEINVERTThe notes
1Am7ROOTA3 C4 E4 G4
2Fmaj71STA3 C4 E4 F4
3Dm72NDA3 C4 D4 F4
4Em71STG3 B3 D4 E4

Look down the last column. Each chord is turned over (INVERT) until it sits as close to the one before as it can: from A minor 7 to F major 7 only one note moves, G down to F; to D minor 7, one more, E down to D; to E minor 7, three notes step down while D stays put. That's the voice leading of Track 1 again, all the way round, and it's why four chords can change under the music without anyone hearing them jump. Try bar 2 at INVERT ROOT and hear the difference: F major 7 drops to F3 and the progression lurches.

Listen to the second chord, too. Three of the four are minor, and F major 7 is the only major one. That's the lift in bar 2, the moment the loop seems to look up, before D minor 7 and E minor 7 bring it back down to A. Major and minor, bright and dark, in four bars, and it never stops going round.

5.12 The bass

The bass plays the same bar as Track 1, on each chord's root: A, F, D, E. Write bar 1 and copy it out to four bars, then move bars 2 to 4 to their roots.

  • 1On TRACKS, turn to track 4; on ENTRY, BAR to 1, LENGTH 1/8, and on VOLT, as in Track 1: rest, A2, rest, A2, rest, A2, rest, A3.
  • 24BAR back one, then COPY›hold4: bar 1 to bar 2.
  • 3Turn END on 4 beats and TO on 4, and hold4: bars 1 and 2 to bars 3 and 4.
  • 4Push encoder 1 for TRANSPOSE, then a bar at a time:
BarTurnSEMITONESBecomes
2START on 4-4F
3END on 4, then START on 4+5D
4END on 4, then START on 4-5E

hold4 after each. (When you open COPY again later, it starts on COPY, whatever you used last.)

Most of the time the bass plays the root, the note a chord is named after, because that's what holds the chord down and tells your ear what it is. But it doesn't have to. The CHORD page names every note of the chord, so you have a choice of four. Try bar 2's bass on A instead of F, SEMITONES 0 instead of -4: F major 7 over an A sounds softer, less settled, almost like A minor again. Musicians write that as F/A, "F over A", and call it a slash chord. Any of a chord's notes can go in the bass, and each one gives it a different colour.

5.13 Playing Track 2

Play it as you played Track 1 (section 5.8, figure figure 5.2): kick and open hats, then the clap and the swung hats, the bass, the chords at bar 25, the breakdown with Ember's filter, everything, and the drums to finish. This time, in the breakdown, the chords are on their own long enough to hear the whole progression come round twice as the filter opens.

Try this

Find a progression of your own. Search for one, or take one from a song you love, and write it on track 5 in place of these four, a bar each. Keep the bass on the roots to start with, then try other notes of the chords under it. If a chord sounds too far from its neighbours, try INVERT until it sits close.

5.14 Track 3: your own, and a whole song

So far, every third track has been the second one with your own choices on top. This one has those too, but it also brings in one more new thing, because it belongs with house: building a whole song, written out from the first bar to the last, so that it plays itself. Section 5.17 has one way it might go, written out by us to show the method, not to be the song: the song is the one you write out.

Start from Track 2

  • 1On STEP, load house Track 2, then SONG›4ACTION›DUPLICATE›hold4, and name the copy.
  • 2On TRACKS, unmute any track that says MUTED.

Choices

  • ·The tempo, between about 118 and 128: deep house sits at the slow end, the jumpier kinds at the fast end.
  • ·The swing. A click or two either way on TEMPO's SWING changes the whole feel.
  • ·The chords. Another sound on Ember (HOUSE ORGAN, E PIANO), or a progression of your own on track 5, found by ear or borrowed.
  • ·The bass. Other notes of the chords under them (section 5.12), or another Volt sound: FUNK BASS, ROUND BASS.
  • ·The kit. BOOM for a deeper, rounder kick under the same patterns.

Make your choices first. The next section writes everything out, and it's easiest to change a sound or a chord while each part is still four bars long.

5.15 Writing the whole song out

Until now you've arranged tracks by muting and unmuting them as they play. That's how a lot of dance music is made, and it's live and fun, but the arrangement is in your hands, not in the song: play it again and you have to do it all again. The other way is to write the song out, every part in every bar where it should play, and then it plays itself, the same every time, and you can change one bar without touching the rest.

Step is built for that. A song on Step is one long timeline of bars, like a score: it doesn't hold "patterns" or "parts", only notes at their places. A track's own loop (LOOP 1 BAR) is the exception, repeating by itself for the whole song, and that's why a written-out song starts by giving those tracks up.

Every track four bars long

The drums are one-bar loops on tracks 1, 2, 3 and 6. Make each one an ordinary four-bar track, like the bass and the chords. For each of those four tracks:

  • 1On TRACKS, turn to the track and turn encoder 3, LOOP, down one click, from 1 BAR to AUTO.
  • 2ENTRY›4BAR›1, then COPY: the range is bar 1.
  • 3Push encoder 1 three times, past TRANSPOSE and DELETE, to FILL.
  • 4Turn encoder 2, UNTIL, on 12 beats, to 4:4.1, the last beat of bar 4. Encoder 1's box says 3 TIMES. Then hold2.

FILL repeats the range, end to end, after itself, until UNTIL: bar 1 copied into bars 2, 3 and 4 in one go. Now all six tracks are four bars long, and together they're one four-bar block of everything.

Sixty-four bars

SECTIONS is COPY's work on every AUTO track at once. On STEP, press SONG, then SONG again: the top bar says SECTIONS. Then:

  • 1The range starts as bar 1. Turn encoder 4, END, on 3 bars, to bar 4.
  • 2Push encoder 1 three times, to FILL.
  • 3Turn encoder 2, UNTIL, until it says 64:1.1, bar 64. (It turns a bar a click; turn it quickly and it speeds up.)
  • 4hold2. The screen says how many notes it wrote.

That's the four-bar block sixteen times over: 64 bars, about 1,800 notes, every part playing all the way through.

Carving the arrangement out

Now take away what shouldn't be there, the way a sculptor takes away stone. On each track below, on ENTRY move BAR to 1, press COPY, push encoder 1 twice to DELETE, turn END on to the last bar's last beat, then START on to the first bar, and hold4. (Turn END first: START can't go past it. They move a beat a click, so turn quickly.)

TrackBarsEND onSTART onWhy

Play it now, from the start, and don't touch anything: the intro, the bass and chords arriving at bar 17, the breakdown at 41 and the return at 49, all on their own. To change the arrangement later, delete some more, or copy a bar back from somewhere else. The song is yours to edit bar by bar.

Room for a whole song

A song has room for 8,192 notes, shared by all its tracks, so a busy track can take thousands. If you ever fill it, COPY and FILL say SONG FULL, and how many notes went in.

5.16 The pump, if you have Haze

Listen to a French house record from the late 1990s and you'll hear the music breathe: everything but the kick dips every time the kick lands and swells back between, so the whole track seems to pump. In a studio it's done with a compressor on the music, keyed by the kick, called sidechain compression or ducking. Haze does it with PUMP: it turns one synth down whenever another plays.

  • 1Join Haze to the end of the chain.
  • 2On HAZE, press the 12th white key from the top: the screen says PUMP.
  • 3The preset sends every synth into its reverb. Keep it on the chords only: SENDS, and turn STRIKE and VOLT to 0.
  • 4SOURCE, and turn encoder 1, SYNTH, a click at a time until it says EMBER: the synth that pumps.
  • 5PUMP, and turn encoder 1, KEY, to STRIKE: what it pumps to.

DEPTH is how far the chords dip, RELEASE how quickly they come back. The pump follows Strike, so the claps and hats push the chords down too, but it's the kick, four times a bar, that you hear breathing.

5.18 What you've learned

  • ·Chords two ways, by hand and by name on the CHORD page; sevenths, inversions, and voice leading.
  • ·Chord progressions: borrowing them, Roman numerals, major and minor, and that if it sounds good, it is good.
  • ·The bass on the roots, and slash chords when it isn't.
  • ·Swing, and why it needs notes on the semiquavers it moves; open and closed hats together.
  • ·REMEMBER SOUNDS.
  • ·A song written out: FILL, SECTIONS, and carving an arrangement with DELETE.
  • ·Haze's PUMP: one synth breathing with another.

Next, hip-hop: samples, chopped and replayed, and in its third track, your own voice.

Chapter 6 - Hip-hop

A drum break cut into pieces and put back together, a bass that nods, and room left for a voice.

Every other kind of music in this book was made by people playing instruments, even if the instruments were machines. Hip-hop began with people playing records. Its first instrument was two turntables, its first sound the best four bars of someone else's song, and it grew into a way of making music out of music: finding a moment on an old record, cutting it out, and building something new on it. This chapter does that on Taste, the sampler.

What you need for this chapter

The Root, Step, Taste, Strike and Volt, joined in that order, and headphones. For Track 3, a microphone in the Root's LINE/MIC IN socket, or the little microphone built into the Root's top.

6.1 Where hip-hop came from

On 11 August 1973, in the recreation room of a block of flats at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue in the Bronx, New York, a young Jamaican-born DJ called Kool Herc played at his sister's back-to-school party. He'd noticed that the dancers went wildest in the break: the few bars of a funk record where the singing and the band stop and only the drummer plays. So he bought two copies of the same records, and played the break on one, then the same break on the other while he spun the first back to its start, over and over, so a ten-second break lasted as long as the dancers wanted. The dancers were the b-boys and b-girls, and the breaks gave breakdancing its name.

Over those breaks, the DJ's friends took the microphone to hype the crowd, and the shouts became rhymes: the MC, the rapper. Grandmaster Flash turned Herc's trick into a precise art, and DJs learned to scratch, cut and juggle records like instruments. For six years it lived only at parties, on street corners and on cassettes. Then in 1979 the Sugarhill Gang's "Rapper's Delight", fifteen minutes of rhymes over a studio band replaying Chic's "Good Times", sold millions, and the world heard rap.

Chapter 2 told how the 808 arrived under hip-hop in 1982. The bigger change came a few years later. Marley Marl, a producer in Queens, found that a sampler could record a single drum hit off a record, and play it back in a new rhythm. Now the break didn't have to be played as it was: it could be cut into pieces and rebuilt. Two machines made that the way hip-hop was made. The E-mu SP-1200 (1987) sampled at 12 bits and 26 kHz, rougher than a CD, with only ten seconds of memory, and its gritty, dark sound became the sound of New York. The Akai MPC60 (1988), designed with Roger Linn, put sixteen rubber pads under the producer's fingers, and a swing setting from his drum machines.

The late 1980s and early 90s are called the golden age. Public Enemy's producers, the Bomb Squad, piled dozens of samples into a single track; De La Soul's 3 Feet High and Rising (1989) borrowed from everything from Steely Dan to French lessons; Pete Rock, DJ Premier and the Wu-Tang Clan's RZA chopped soul and jazz records into beats that are still copied today. KRS-One named that hard, swung sound on an album title in 1993: Return of the Boom Bap, boom for the kick and bap for the snare. Later, J Dilla in Detroit let his drums fall slightly out of time, lazy and loose, as if the beat were leaning on a wall, and changed how a generation hears rhythm; DJ Shadow's Endtroducing..... (1996) was a whole album of beats, made from samples on an MPC60, with no rapping at all.

Whose record is it?

A record belongs to the people who made it, and a sample of it, however short, is a piece of their work. In 1991 a court ruled that Biz Markie had broken the law by sampling a Gilbert O'Sullivan song without asking, and since then hip-hop producers have had to get permission for their samples, and pay for it, before a record comes out, or play the part again themselves. Sample what you like to learn and to practise; ask before you put someone else's recording into anything you share or sell. Everything in this chapter is safe: Taste's starter break was played on Strike and made for Taste, and Track 3's sample is your own voice.

6.2 What hip-hop is made of

Before anything else, the most important thing about a hip-hop beat: it's usually only half of the record.

Most hip-hop is made to go under a rapper. The beat is the stage; the rapper is the show. That's why a beat repeats, why it leaves gaps in the middle of the sound, and why the best ones seem almost too simple on their own: there's a voice still to come. The rapping is the heart of hip-hop, and it belongs to the person doing it, out of their own life, their own streets and their own way of talking. We're a small company who make synthesisers. We know our limits, and we aren't going to try, under any circumstances, to tell anyone how to express themselves in rap. So this chapter builds the stage, and only the stage. If you rap, these are beats for you to rap over. If you don't, they stand up on their own, as plenty of instrumental hip-hop does, and somewhere there's a rapper looking for a beat.

  • ·The tempo. Slow: about 85 to 95, and that's the head-nodding speed. These tracks are at 90.
  • ·A break. The drums come from a recording, sampled and chopped, instead of being played on a drum machine: a kick and a snare, the boom and the bap, with the life of a real kit around them.
  • ·Swing, as in house, but here you feel it more, because the beat is slow enough to hear every semiquaver.
  • ·An 808 kick under the break's own, for a weight you feel in your chest more than hear.
  • ·A short bass line, a bar or two, round and round.
  • ·Room for the voice. The arrangement is built for rapping: verses of sixteen bars, hooks (the choruses) of eight, and moments where the beat drops out so a line can land on its own.

6.3 Track 1 at a glance

Hip-hop Track 1 is boom bap: Taste's starter break, cut into sixteen pieces and played back in a new order at a new tempo, with an 808 kick under it and a two-bar bass line on Volt.

Sound 6.1  Hip-hop Track 1, as built in sections 6.4 to 6.8: Taste's break, chopped into sixteenths and played in a new order at 90, an 808 kick under it, and a two-bar bass on Volt.

6.4 Setting up

A new song, and the sounds

  • 1Join the units in this order from the Root: Step, Taste, Strike, Volt.
  • 2On STEP, SONG›4ACTION›NEW›hold4, and name it.
  • 3On TASTE, SOUNDS›1BANK›FAC A›2SOUND›BREAK CHOP.
  • 4On STRIKE, BOOM.
  • 5On VOLT, SOUNDS›1BANK›FAC A›2SOUND›FUNK BASS, and press OCT- once.

Tempo, swing and three tracks

  • 1On STEP, TEMPO›1TEMPO›90, then turn encoder 3, SWING, up 7 clicks, to 57%.
  • 2On TRACKS, give each track its unit with encoder 2: track 1 TASTE, track 2 STRIKE, track 3 VOLT.
  • 3LOOP 1 BAR for tracks 1 and 2; leave track 3 on AUTO.

Swing at 57% is a little less than house's 58%, but at 90 beats a minute every semiquaver lasts much longer, so the same lean is easier to hear. Those percentages, by the way, come from Roger Linn's drum machines and the MPC: hip-hop producers talk about "a 57 swing" or "a 62 swing" the way guitarists talk about strings.

6.5 The break, chopped

Sixteen pieces

BREAK CHOP is one bar of drums, recorded at 95 beats a minute, and already cut into sixteen pieces, one for each semiquaver, laid out on sixteen keys in order from the top: the first semiquaver on C3, the next on C#3, and so on, black keys and white, to D#4. Press them one after another, slowly, and you'll hear the bar go by a piece at a time. Each piece is called a slice, or a chop.

KeyC3C#3D3D#3E3F3F#3G3
Slice12345678
KeyG#3A3A#3B3C4C#4D4D#4
Slice910111213141516

To see one, press TRIM and a key: the screen shows the whole bar with that slice marked out, and its name at the top.

Why chop it?

Here's the old problem with samples. Play a recording faster and it goes up in pitch; slower, and it goes down, like a record on the wrong speed. The break was played at 95 and this song is at 90. Slow the whole bar down to fit, and every drum drops in pitch and goes woolly.

Chopped, it doesn't have to. Step plays each slice at its own place in the bar, at 90, and each one plays at its own speed and pitch, as recorded. The slices are a little shorter than a semiquaver at 90, so each one finishes a moment before the next begins, and you never hear the join. The break now plays at any tempo you like, and it can play in any order you like too. That's the trick the SP-1200's owners found.

A new order

On STEP, ENTRY, LENGTH 1/16, BAR at 1. On TASTE, press these sixteen keys in turn, the first four in each row being a beat:

Beat 1C3C#3D3D#3
Beat 2E3F3C3G3
Beat 3G#3C#3A#3B3
Beat 4C4F3D4D#4

It's the break almost as it was, slices 1 to 16, with three changed (in bold). The one you'll notice is the third semiquaver of beat 2: slice 1, the first kick of the bar, played again, so a kick lands just before beat 3 and pushes the beat forward. The other two swap a slice that's only the ring of a hit for another one, so they change the colour of the hi-hats, not the rhythm. Try your own: anything that sounds good is right, and figure figure 6.1 shows what's on every key.

Musicians count the four semiquavers of a beat "one-e-and-a", "two-e-and-a"; that extra kick is on the "and" of two. You'll hear producers talk like that.

6.6 The 808, and the bass

Under the break

The break's kick is a real-sounding kick, tight and quick. Hip-hop often puts an 808 underneath it, for the long low boom no recorded kit has.

  • 1On TRACKS, turn to track 2; on ENTRY, BAR back to 1, and VELO down to 80.
  • 2LENGTH is still 1/16. On STRIKE: KICK, nine rests, KICK, five rests: semiquavers 1 and 11, the first kick of the bar and the one on the "and" of three.
  • 3VELO back up to 100.

Two kicks a bar, on two of the break's own, and soft: that's layering, two sounds played together as one. The break gives the kick its click and its life, the 808 its weight. Listen with track 2 muted and unmuted: you'll hardly hear the 808 as a separate drum at all, only the floor dropping lower.

The bass

Track 3, LENGTH 1/8, BAR at 1, on VOLT, two bars:

Bar 1D2restrestD2restF2G2rest
Bar 2A2restrestA2restG2F2rest

D, F, G and A are four notes of D minor's scale, and the line climbs up through them in bar 1 and falls back in bar 2, a slow nod, like the listeners' heads. FUNK BASS is round and short, so the rests between the notes are real silences, and the break shows through them.

6.7 Balance, and remembering the sounds

On STEP, MIXER: TASTE at 0, STRIKE down to -6, VOLT down to -3. The break leads, as the drums lead in every kind of hip-hop; the 808 is felt under it; the bass sits just behind.

Then, as in house, SONG›4ACTION›REMEMBER SOUNDS›hold4, so the song brings Taste's break, Strike's kit and Volt's bass back whenever you load it.

On TRACKS, mute tracks 2 and 3, so only the break plays, and press PLAY.

Hip-hop Track 2 is Track 1 made dustier and longer: Taste's sound made gritty like the old samplers, a two-bar beat with a fill at the end, a four-bar bass line, and soft swung hats.

6.10 Setting up

  • 1On STEP, load hip-hop Track 1, then SONG›4ACTION›DUPLICATE›hold4, and name the copy.

6.11 Twelve bits

On TASTE, press CHARACTER, the top button on the right, and turn encoder 1 two clicks, to 12-BIT 26K.

Listen to the break change: darker, grainier, a little crunchy round the snare. That's Taste playing its sound back the way the SP-1200 did. A sampler stores a sound as a long row of numbers, thousands a second, each one the height of the wave at that moment. A CD uses 16 bits for each number, so the heights come in 65,536 steps; 12 bits give only 4,096, and the coarser steps add a faint fizz. And 26,000 numbers a second instead of 44,100 can't hold the very top of the sound, so the cymbals go dull and a metallic edge creeps in. On paper it's worse. To a generation of listeners it was the sound of hip-hop, and producers with far better machines still choose it. The middle choice, 12-BIT, is the MPC60's: gritty, with more of the top left in.

Keeping it

There's a star in Taste's top bar: you've changed a factory sound, and a factory sound is never changed for good. That matters here, because when you press PLAY from the start Step chooses each remembered sound again, and choosing a sound drops any changes to it. So make the gritty break a sound of your own:

  • 1On TASTE, SOUNDS, and hold3, COPY TO. It copies what you're hearing, 12 bits and all, into USER A 01, and Taste is now playing your copy.
  • 2On STEP, SONG›4ACTION›REMEMBER SOUNDS›hold4, so the song remembers your copy instead of the factory break.

6.12 Two bars of beat, four of bass

The beat, with a fill

A beat that's the same every bar starts to sound like a machine. A drummer keeps the groove but adds something at the end of a phrase, a little roll or an extra snare, to say "here comes the next one": a fill.

  • 1Clear track 1: TRACKS›1TRACK›1›hold4. Then turn encoder 3, LOOP, up one click, to 2 BARS.
  • 2On ENTRY, BAR to 1, LENGTH 1/16, and on TASTE write bar 1 as in Track 1 (section 6.5), then carry straight on into bar 2:
Bar 2, beat 1C3C#3D3D#3
Beat 2E3F3C3G3
Beat 3G#3A3A#3G3
Beat 4C4D#4C4D#4

The first half of bar 2 is bar 1 again. Then slice 8, a ghost snare, comes early, and the last beat is snare, ghost, snare, ghost: the snare doubled, tumbling over the bar line into bar 1.

Four bars of bass

  • 1On TRACKS, turn to track 3; on ENTRY, BAR to 1, and press COPY: the range is bar 1.
  • 2Turn END on 4 beats and TO on 4: bars 1 and 2 will be copied to bars 3 and 4. hold4.
  • 3Push encoder 1 for TRANSPOSE. Turn END on 8 beats, then START on 8, so the range is bars 3 and 4, SEMITONES to +5, and hold4.

Bars 3 and 4 are now up five semitones, a fourth, from D to G, the same move as house Track 1's bass. Two bars in D minor, two in G minor: the line goes away and comes home, and it takes four bars to come round, so a verse of sixteen goes round it four times.

Swung hats

  • 1On TRACKS, turn to track 4, give it STRIKE, and LOOP 1 BAR.
  • 2On ENTRY, BAR to 1, VELO down to 60, LENGTH 1/16, and on STRIKE, four times over: rest, CL HAT, rest, CL HAT. Then VELO back to 100.

Soft hats on the "e" and the "a" of every beat, the semiquavers the swing moves, as in house Track 1. The break has hats of its own, and these sit between them, very quietly: you'll feel the beat lean back further before you hear them.

6.14 Track 3: your own voice

Every third track so far has been yours to choose. This one is yours more than any: you'll record your own voice on Taste, cut it into words, and play the words as a hook, the catchy line that comes round between verses. Not a rap: a few words, chopped and played as an instrument, the way producers have chopped voices off records since the 1980s. Section 6.18 has one way it might go, and an apology.

Start from Track 2

  • 1On STEP, load hip-hop Track 2, then SONG›4ACTION›DUPLICATE›hold4, and name the copy.
  • 2On TRACKS, unmute any track that says MUTED.

Taste is still playing USER A 01, the copy you made in section 6.11. That matters: a recording always goes into a sound of your own, never a factory one. (If you try to record onto a factory sound, the screen says COPY IT TO RECORD.)

What to say

Think of four to six short words, or a short phrase, and say them with a clear gap after each one, about half a second: the gaps are how Taste will find the words. Anything you like. A name, a place, a line of your own, the sound of a word you like saying.

6.15 Recording

  • 1On TASTE, press E4, the key just after the break's sixteen. That's where the recording will go.
  • 2Press SAMPLE, the top button on the left.
  • 3Turn encoder 1, SOURCE, one click to MIC IN, for a microphone in the Root's LINE/MIC IN socket, or two to BUILT-IN MIC for the one in the Root's top. (SOURCE moves one choice a click, however fast you turn it.)
  • 4Turn encoder 2, THRESH, up eleven clicks, to -30 DB.

THRESH is the threshold: how loud a sound must be to start the recording. At -30 DB, Taste waits through the hum of the room and starts the moment you speak, so the recording begins exactly on your first word. Say something now and watch the bar under the middle of the screen: it's how loud the microphone hears you. The red mark is the threshold, and your words should go well past it.

  • 5Push encoder 4, REC. It says WAITING.
  • 6Say your words, with the gaps.
  • 7Push encoder 4 again, STOP.

Your voice is on E4: press it and you'll hear the whole recording. If it's too quiet, or cut off, or you just want another go, push REC and record again: each take replaces the last.

6.16 Chopping, and loudness

A word on each key

The break was cut into even sixteenths, because drums play in time. Words don't, so Taste cuts them where they start.

  • 1Press CHOP, the fourth button down on the left.
  • 2Turn encoder 2, MODE, one click to AT HITS.
  • 3Turn encoder 3, SENS, right down to 0.0. (It moves a tenth a click: turn quickly.)
  • 4hold4, CHOP.

Taste listens through the recording for each sudden jump in loudness, the start of a word, and cuts there: one slice on E4, the next on F4, the next on F#4, and on up the keys, black and white. Press them in turn and your words come back one at a time. SENS is how small a jump counts. At 0.0 only the big ones do, the starts of words after a gap; turn it up and Taste cuts at smaller jumps too, the hard sounds inside a word, a K or a T, so the words split into pieces. If two words have come out on one key, leave a longer gap between them; if a word has split in two, try SENS a little lower. Either way, press E4, record again on SAMPLE, and chop again: CHOP always cuts from the key you're on.

As loud as it goes

A voice into a microphone usually comes out quieter than the break. Press MIX, the fifth button in the middle column, and hold4, NORMAL. Taste turns the recording up until its loudest moment is as loud as a sound can be, and says how much louder it made it. The screen then says FULL.

6.17 The hook

  • 1On STEP, on TRACKS, turn to track 5, give it TASTE, and turn LOOP up two clicks, to 2 BARS.
  • 2On ENTRY, BAR to 1, LENGTH 1/8, and play your words in on Taste's keys, with rests between, across two bars.

Our six words went like this, a key each:

Bar 1E4restrestrestF4F#4restrest
Bar 2G4restG#4restA4restrestrest

One word, a gap, two together, then the last three spaced out, each word starting on a quaver, in time with the break. That's what chopping a voice gives you that a recording doesn't: the words fall exactly on the beat, in any order you choose, as often as you like. Play one word three times in a row, or the last word first.

Then on TRACKS mute tracks 2, 3 and 4, so the song starts with the beat and the voice alone.

6.18 One way it might go

Here's ours, and we owe you an explanation.

To make an example for the book, we needed a voice, and the only one in the building that would say the words on demand, take after take, without getting embarrassed, was a computer's: the speaking voice built into an ordinary laptop, reading "Yeah. Check it. Make some noise." in the tone of a railway station announcement. It was recorded exactly as section 6.15 tells you to record yours, through the Root's mic input, then chopped AT HITS and played on track 5. If you remember the BBC's Look Around You and its "Music 2000" competition, you'll know what's coming. We're sorry. We did say we knew our limits.

Sound 6.3  Hip-hop Track 3, one way it might go: Track 2 with a voice recorded on Taste, chopped into words and played as a hook. The voice is a laptop's built-in speech standing in for yours, and we apologise.

BarsAs it starts
1-4The beat and the voice.
5-8Mute track 5; unmute tracks 2 and 4: the 808 and the hats.
9-24Unmute track 3: the first verse.
25-28Mute tracks 1 and 4; unmute track 5: the 808, the bass and the voice.
29-36Unmute tracks 1 and 4: the hook, everything.
37-52Mute track 5: the second verse.
53-60Unmute track 5: the hook again.
61-64Mute tracks 2, 3 and 4: the beat and the voice, as it began. STOP at the end of bar 64.

Listen anyway, because it makes the point of this chapter better than we could. Everything else in this book can be written down: every press, every setting, every track, which is why your Track 1 sounds like ours. Your voice can't be. Once it's on Taste, saying your words in your way, you're off the edge of our map, and that's where the music starts. You'll be more creative off the book than this book could ever be. Put your voice where our laptop's is, and you'll hear the difference straight away.

Try this

Record other sounds onto the keys after your words: a hand clap, a cough, a tap on a mug, a friend saying one word. Chop them AT HITS and drop them into the beat on a track of their own. And if you know someone who raps, you have a beat for them now.

6.19 What you've learned

  • ·Where hip-hop came from: breaks, DJs, MCs, and the samplers that cut records into pieces; and that a sample of someone's record needs their permission.
  • ·That a beat is a stage, and its arrangement leaves room for a voice: verses, hooks and drop-outs, in fours.
  • ·Chops: a break sliced into semiquavers, played at a new tempo without changing its pitch, and in a new order.
  • ·Layering an 808 under a recorded kick; swing on a slow beat; a two-bar beat with a fill.
  • ·Bits and sample rates, and why 12 bits at 26 kHz still sounds right.
  • ·Keeping a changed factory sound as a sound of your own, so REMEMBER SOUNDS keeps it too.
  • ·Recording on Taste: SOURCE, THRESH, REC; chopping AT HITS with SENS; NORMAL.

Next, ambient: music with no beat at all, made of slowly drifting sound.

Chapter 7 - Ambient

No beat, no verse and no chorus: chords that drift past each other, a cloud of grains, and a lot of space.

Every chapter so far has had a beat to hold on to. This one lets go of it. Ambient music doesn't march, or dance, or tell a story with a beginning and an end. You can listen to it closely, or leave it playing at the edge of the room while you do something else, and it's meant to work both ways. It's made of the things the rest of this book used as decoration: long notes, slow change, and space. On Step it's made of loops that never line up.

What you need for this chapter

The Root, Step, Glass, Haze and Grit, joined in that order, and headphones. Haze hears every unit wherever it is in the row, with one exception: a unit that is itself listening to the chain, as Grit does, adds its sound on the way back, so Haze hears it only if it's on Haze's right. Haze goes to the left of Grit so its reverb takes in Grit's grains as well as Glass. For Track 3, Axis too, on the end of the row; if you don't have one, Glass can play Track 3 on EVOLUTION (in its FAC D bank).

7.1 Where ambient came from

In 1917 the French composer Erik Satie wrote what he called musique d'ameublement, furniture music: short pieces to be repeated over and over in the background, like wallpaper, while people talked. At its first performance, in 1920, the audience politely stopped talking to listen, and Satie walked round the room telling them to carry on chatting. He was fifty years early.

In 1975 Brian Eno was lying in bed recovering from a road accident when a friend put on a record of harp music for him. One speaker wasn't working and the volume was very low, and he was too sore to get up and fix it. So he lay there hearing the harp mixed with the rain outside, barely there, and realised he liked it that way: music as part of the room, as much a colour as a tune. His records Discreet Music (1975) and Ambient 1: Music for Airports (1978) gave it a name. Music for Airports is made from tape loops of different lengths, each with a single sung note or a short piano phrase on it, all playing at once, so the notes drift together and apart and never meet the same way twice. That's exactly what this chapter's tracks do on Step. The second record of the series, The Plateaux of Mirror (1980), was made with the pianist Harold Budd, all slow chords soaked in echo.

In the 1990s ambient came back through the dance floor, as the chapter 2 history said: in the chill-out rooms of raves, and on records such as the KLF's Chill Out (1990) and Aphex Twin's Selected Ambient Works 85-92 (1992), made by a teenager in Cornwall on home-built and second-hand synths. It has never gone away since: long, slow pieces that play for hours, and apps that make music which never ends.

7.2 The room next door

Ambient has a family on the other side of the wall, in the concert hall and the studio, and you'll hear more of what's possible on these units by listening to them than to almost anything else. None of this is background music. Most of it asks you to listen harder than any dance record does. But it's where long sounds, slowly changing textures, grains, drones and strange harmony were first worked out, and the crossover with ambient, and with everything in this chapter, is real. Here are ten places to start, with what each one has to do with your units.

  • Edgard Varèse called music "organised sound", and meant any sound at all. Chapter 2 met the Philips Pavilion at the 1958 Brussels World's Fair; the piece he made for its hundreds of loudspeakers was Poème électronique. Listen to Ionisation (1931) too, for percussion alone.
  • Iannis Xenakis designed that pavilion, working as an architect in Le Corbusier's office, and made the piece played between the shows in it, Concret PH (1958): the crackle of burning charcoal, recorded, cut into tiny pieces and piled up into clouds. He was one of the first to think of sound as grains, which is what Grit does. His orchestral Metastaseis (1954) has dozens of strings sliding, each on its own line, into great moving masses.
  • György Ligeti's Atmosphères (1961) has no melody and no beat at all, only enormous chords of notes packed side by side, shifting so slowly you notice only that something has changed. If you've seen Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey, you've heard it. Track 2's clusters come from here.
  • Karlheinz Stockhausen's Stimmung (1968) is six singers on a single chord for about seventy minutes, singing its overtones, the notes hidden inside a note, so the one chord shimmers with colours. It might be the most ambient piece ever written for a concert hall.
  • Éliane Radigue worked in Paris with the inventors of musique concrète, then spent decades making long, slow drones on a modular synthesiser and tape, pieces in which a sound changes so gradually that you can't hear it change, only find that it has. Start with Trilogie de la Mort (1988-93). It's the closest thing there is to this chapter played with infinite patience.
  • Pauline Oliveros made tape music in San Francisco in the 1960s and then turned to listening itself: she called her practice Deep Listening, listening to everything, all the time. Her album Deep Listening (1989) was recorded with two friends at the bottom of an empty underground water tank, whose echo lasted 45 seconds. When you turn Haze to CAVE in Track 3, think of her.
  • Laurie Spiegel made The Expanding Universe (1980) on a room-sized computer system at Bell Labs: slow, glowing music in which simple rules let the notes find their own way, as Step's loops do here. A piece of hers is on the gold records the Voyager spacecraft carried out of the solar system in 1977.
  • Hildegard Westerkamp makes soundscape compositions from recordings of real places. In Kits Beach Soundwalk (1989) she walks you along a beach in Vancouver, talking quietly, filtering the city's roar until you can hear the tiny clicks of barnacles. The storm in Track 3 is a very small step in her direction.
  • Trevor Wishart, from Leeds, transforms sounds into other sounds: in Red Bird (1977) words melt into birdsong and the noises of machines. His Vox cycle (1980-88) does it with voices, and his book On Sonic Art is one of the best ever written about sound. If you liked chopping your voice in chapter 6, he's where that road leads.
  • And for the clusters, the first of them: Henry Cowell, who in The Tides of Manaunaun (1917) told the pianist to press the low keys with a whole forearm.

Put one on, turn the lights down, and don't do anything else for a while. Then come back and make something.

7.3 What ambient is made of

  • ·No beat you can dance to. Step still has a tempo, and it still counts bars, but nothing plays on the beat. These tracks are at 70 and 60.
  • ·Long notes, and space between them. Silence is part of the music, and a sound is allowed to fade all the way out.
  • ·Loops that never line up. Each part goes round on a loop of its own length, so the parts keep meeting in new ways. It's acid Track 2's three beats against four, made into the whole method.
  • ·Reverb and echo as instruments. Here Haze isn't the finishing touch: it's half of the sound.
  • ·Harmony that floats. With no chord progression to follow, the chords are free to be strange: notes rubbing against each other, packed together, or from no ordinary scale at all. Nothing needs to resolve, because nothing is going anywhere.

7.4 Track 1 at a glance

Ambient Track 1 is five chords on Glass's electric piano, each on a loop of a different length, echoing into a hall.

7.5 Setting up

  • 1Join the units in this order from the Root: Step, Glass, Haze, Grit.
  • 2On STEP, SONG›4ACTION›NEW›hold4, and name it.
  • 3On GLASS, SOUNDS›1BANK›FAC A›2SOUND›E.PIANO 1.
  • 4On STEP, TEMPO›1TEMPO›70.

Five loops of their own

On TRACKS, give tracks 1 to 5 to GLASS with encoder 2. Then, on each track, push encoder 3, LOOP, so it counts in beats (the screen says BARS + BEATS underneath), and turn it on to the track's length:

Track12345
Beats1719232931
LOOP says4+14+35+37+17+3

Why those numbers? They're all prime numbers, which nothing divides into but themselves and 1. Two loops of 16 and 8 beats line up every 16 beats, so you'd hear the same meeting over and over. Loops of 17 and 19 beats line up only every 323 beats, and all five of these only every 6.6 million beats, which at this tempo is about two months. So in practice the chords never meet the same way twice. Eno's tape loops in Music for Airports were cut to lengths like that for the same reason.

7.6 Five chords

Each track has one chord, written by holding its four keys on Glass together and letting them all go, as you did for techno Track 3's stab. A few crotchet rests before each one start the loops off at different moments, so they don't all begin together.

On STEP, ENTRY, then, a track at a time, BAR back to 1 each time:

TrackRests (LENGTH 1/4)Then LENGTH 1/2, the chordWhat it is
1noneD3 A3 E4 F4D minor, with E and F a semitone apart at the top
22E3 A3 D4 G4fourths, stacked
35F3 C4 E4 G4F major 9, with no third
49B3 C4 E4 A4A minor, with B and C rubbing underneath
513G3 B3 C#4 F#4G Lydian: the odd one out

Play each one on its own before you write it, and listen to what makes it strange. Track 1's chord is D minor, but its top two notes, E and F, are side by side on the keyboard, a semitone apart, and they rub against each other like two strings slightly out of tune. Track 4 has its rub at the bottom. Track 2 isn't built in thirds, every other note, like most chords, but in fourths: E, A, D, G, open and hollow, the sound of a lot of jazz and film music. Track 3 leaves out F major's third, A, the note that says major or minor, so it's neither. And Track 5 brings in C# and F#, notes none of the other chords have. It's built on the Lydian scale, a major scale with its fourth note raised, which sounds bright and slightly unearthly; but the moment it meets track 1's F or track 4's C, C# and F# clash with them a semitone apart, and for a few seconds the harmony goes somewhere nobody planned.

That's the point. You've written five chords, but you'll hear dozens, made by whichever ones happen to be sounding together. Some meetings are sweet, some sour, some odd; none of them were written. Figure figure 7.1 shows a couple of minutes of them.

7.7 Space, balance and remembering

  • 1On HAZE, press the 8th white key from the top: the screen says ECHO HALL, an echo that repeats into a big hall.
  • 2SENDS, and turn encoder 1, GLASS, up from 30 to 70: most of Glass goes into the echo.
  • 3On STEP, MIXER, and turn GLASS down to -6. Four-note chords piling up get loud. (MIXER's boxes are the units in order: GLASS, HAZE, GRIT.)
  • 4SONG›4ACTION›REMEMBER SOUNDS›hold4.

7.8 Playing Track 1

On TRACKS, mute tracks 2 to 5, so only track 1 plays, and press PLAY. A bar at 70 lasts nearly three and a half seconds, so there's time; follow the bar number on Step's screen.

At barDo
1Track 1 alone.
3, 5, 7, 9Unmute tracks 2, 3, 4 and 5, one at each.
33, 37, 41, 45Mute them again, in the same order.
48STOP at the end of the bar, and let the echo die away.

Then just listen. There's no chorus coming, and no drop. Notice how differently the same chord sounds depending on what it meets: track 1's D minor alone, then under the fourths, then against the Lydian chord's C#. You'll find yourself waiting for particular meetings, and they won't come when you expect.

Try this

Change a loop's length while it plays, a beat at a time, and hear the meetings change. Make your own chords: start from three notes that sound good and move one of them a semitone, then listen to the rub. Try a sixth track with one low note on a very long loop, 37 or 41 beats. (Glass plays up to sixteen notes at once; if more are asked for, the oldest stop, so long chords on many tracks can cut each other short.)

7.9 Track 2 at a glance

Ambient Track 2 keeps Track 1's loops and gives them denser chords, held for a whole bar on Glass's voices. Grit listens to it all and trails a cloud of grains behind it, and halfway through, the cloud freezes and the chords stop.

7.10 Setting up

  • 1On STEP, load ambient Track 1, then SONG›4ACTION›DUPLICATE›hold4, and name the copy. On TRACKS, unmute any track that says MUTED.
  • 2On GLASS, choose FAC A's VOICE 1 on SOUNDS. (If Glass is already showing SOUNDS, just turn encoder 2: pressing SOUNDS again opens the CARD page.)
  • 3Clear each of the five tracks: TRACKS›1TRACK›1›hold4, then the same for 2, 3, 4 and 5. Clearing takes away a track's notes but keeps its LOOP.

7.11 Clusters

Write the five tracks again on ENTRY, the same rests as Track 1, but each chord with LENGTH 1, a whole bar:

TrackRests (1/4)Then LENGTH 1What it is
1noneA3 B3 C4 D4a cluster: four notes side by side
22E4 F4 G4 A4another, higher
35C3 G3 D4open fifths, holding the others down
49F#4 G#4 A#4 C5whole tones
513D3 G#3 C4 F#4tritones, stacked

A cluster is a chord of notes packed side by side instead of spread out: Cowell's forearm on the keys, Ligeti's Atmosphères. On a piano it's a thud; on held voices, with reverb, it becomes a single shimmering colour, beating gently inside as the close notes rub. Track 3's open fifths, C, G and D, a fifth apart each, give the ear something solid to stand on. Track 4 is four notes a whole tone apart, from the whole-tone scale, six notes all a tone apart, that Claude Debussy used to make music that seems to float with no home key. And Track 5 stacks tritones: D to G#, C to F#, the interval exactly half an octave, which musicians once nicknamed the devil in music. Together, sounding in shifting combinations, these give harmony you won't find in any song, and in ambient that's exactly the point.

Then on STEP, MIXER, and turn GLASS up two clicks, to -4: the voices are softer than the piano.

7.12 A cloud of grains

  • 1On GRIT, SOUNDS›1BANK›FAC A›2SOUND›LIVE CLOUD.
  • 2On HAZE, SENDS: GLASS down to 50, GRIT up to 70.
  • 3On STEP, SONG›4ACTION›REMEMBER SOUNDS›hold4.
  • 4On GRIT, press PLACE, ready for later.

LIVE CLOUD listens to everything on the chain, keeps the last few seconds of it, and plays it back as a haze of tiny overlapping grains, each a fraction of a second long, about a second behind. So everything Glass plays comes back blurred, like breath on a window, and that's what Xenakis heard in his charcoal.

7.13 Playing Track 2, and freezing it

On TRACKS, mute tracks 2 to 5, press PLAY, and bring them in as in Track 1. Then, in the middle, the freeze:

At barDo
1Track 1 alone.
3, 5, 7, 9Unmute tracks 2, 3, 4 and 5.
Just before 29On GRIT, press FREEZE, the top button on the right, and turn encoder 2, SCAN, down 20 clicks, to 0%. Then on STEP mute all five tracks.
37On GRIT, SCAN back up to 100%, and FREEZE again. On STEP, unmute all five.
41, 45, 49, 53Mute tracks 2, 3, 4 and 5 again.
56STOP at the end of the bar.

FREEZE stops Grit listening: the last few seconds it heard are held, and the grains go on playing from them. SCAN is how fast the grains move through that sound, 100% as fast as it happened, 0% not at all, so at 0% the frozen moment simply goes on, a chord caught in mid-air and held. For eight bars the chords have stopped and there's only that frozen cloud and its reverb. Then they come back, Grit lets go, and the cloud starts following them again.

Try this

During the freeze, turn SCAN slowly up and down, or below 0%, so the frozen sound plays backwards, and try SPRAY on encoder 3. Freeze at a different moment and catch a different chord. Try Grit's other live sounds, LIVE ICE and LIVE SHINE.

7.14 Track 3: your own

Duplicate Track 2 and make it yours. Section 7.16 has one way it might go, and section 7.15 the new things it uses. Ambient is the easiest music in the world to make beautifully dull, and ours is a careful demonstration of the parts, not of what they can do; the composers in section 7.2 show what they can do.

  • ·The tempo. Slower is often better: everything stretches out. 60 or below.
  • ·The chords, your own, as dense or as odd as you dare. Move one note of a chord a semitone and listen.
  • ·The loops. Other primes: 37, 41, 43, 47. Or give a track a second chord, so its loop becomes a little phrase.
  • ·The space. Haze's other reverbs, CAVE, BIG HALL, AMBIENT, and how much of each sound you send into them.
  • ·A place. Grit's sounds that play by themselves, such as RAIN CLOUD or FAR STORM, set the music somewhere, as Westerkamp's recordings do.

7.15 A warmer pad, and a storm far off

Moving the tracks to Axis

Glass is a bright instrument, good at bells, pianos and glass. For a warm, soft pad, Axis is the better choice, and you don't have to write anything again to use it: a track can play any unit.

  • 1Join Axis to the right-hand end of the row, after Grit.
  • 2On STEP, on TRACKS, for each of tracks 1 to 5, turn encoder 2, UNIT, on from GLASS to AXIS. The notes stay; Axis plays them now.
  • 3On AXIS, SOUNDS›1BANK›FAC A›2SOUND›AIR PAD.

A touch darker, and a sound of your own

AIR PAD is airy and high, and a little sharp for this. Press FILTER on Axis and turn encoder 1, CUTOFF, down 20 clicks, from 90 to 70: the screen says 3.4 KHZ. The filter takes off everything above that, and the pad goes softer and warmer.

There's now a star in Axis's top bar: a change to a factory sound, which isn't kept, and which REMEMBER SOUNDS would undo every time you press PLAY from the start. So keep it, as you kept Taste's gritty break in chapter 6: on AXIS, SOUNDS›hold3, COPY TO. Your darker AIR PAD is now USER A 01, a sound of your own, and Axis is playing it. Any sound you change and like, on any unit, is worth keeping that way.

Second chords

Give two of the loops a second chord, straight after the first, so they become little two-chord phrases. On ENTRY, for each, BAR to 1, LENGTH 1/4, BAR on past the rests and the first chord, then LENGTH 1 and the chord, on Axis's keys:

TrackBAR onThen the chord
26 clicksD4 E4 G4 A4
413 clicksE4 F#4 G#4 B4

The storm, and the cave

  • 1On GRIT, choose FAC A's FAR STORM on SOUNDS: rain and distant thunder, which plays by itself.
  • 2On HAZE, press the 3rd white key from the top, CAVE, the longest reverb, then SENDS and turn GRIT and AXIS to 60.
  • 3On STEP, MIXER: AXIS down to -4, GRIT down to -12.
  • 4SONG›4ACTION›REMEMBER SOUNDS›hold4.

The storm is quiet, and more of it goes into the reverb than the pad's does: that's how to put a sound far away. Close sounds are loud and clear; distant ones are quieter, and you hear more of the space around them than of the sound itself.

7.16 One way it might go

Track 2, duplicated, slower, at 60, moved to Axis's darker AIR PAD, with two second chords, and a storm a long way off in Haze's CAVE.

Sound 7.3  Ambient Track 3, one way it might go: Track 2 at 60, moved to Axis's AIR PAD made darker, with two second chords, and a storm a long way off in Haze's CAVE.

On TRACKS, mute all five tracks, and press PLAY: the storm starts on its own.

At barDo
1The storm alone.
3, 5, 9, 13, 17Unmute tracks 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, one at each, further and further apart.
29, 33, 37, 41, 45Mute tracks 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1, the other way round.
