The storm plays whether Step is playing or not, so it's faded out by hand. That's often how ambient pieces end: not with a final chord, but by going away.

7.17 What you've learned

  • ·Where ambient came from, Satie to Eno to the chill-out room, and the composers next door: Varèse, Xenakis, Ligeti, Stockhausen, Radigue, Oliveros, Spiegel, Westerkamp, Wishart, Cowell.
  • ·Loops of different lengths on every track, in beats, and why prime numbers never line up.
  • ·Chords that float: semitone rubs, fourths, a missing third, the Lydian scale, clusters, whole tones and tritones; and harmony made by accident, from meetings nobody wrote.
  • ·Clearing a track but keeping its loop; moving tracks to another unit.
  • ·Grit on a live sound, FREEZE, and SCAN.
  • ·A filter to darken a sound, and keeping a changed sound as your own.
  • ·Distance: quieter, and more reverb than sound.

Next, the opposite: jungle and drum and bass, breaks at twice the speed and a bass you feel in your chest.

Chapter 8 - Jungle and drum and bass

A break sped up until it blurs, cut up and thrown about, over a bass that moves at half the speed.

Chapter 6 cut a break into pieces and put it back together at 90. This chapter does the same thing at almost twice the speed, and it changes everything. A funk drummer's few bars, sped up until they blur, cut up and rearranged faster than any drummer could play, over a bass line moving at half the speed, deep enough to feel in your chest: that's jungle, and drum and bass is what it grew into.

What you need for this chapter

The Root, Step, Taste, Strike, Volt and Haze, joined in that order, and headphones. Haze comes in with Track 2.

8.1 Where jungle came from

By 1991 the British rave scene of chapter 2 was speeding up. Its producers, many of them teenagers with a sampler, a computer and a pair of turntables, took the breaks hip-hop had dug up and played them faster and faster, over the basslines of the reggae sound systems they'd grown up with in London, Bristol and Birmingham. The music was called hardcore, then breakbeat hardcore, and around 1992 to 1994 it became jungle: breaks at 160 to 170 beats a minute, chopped and rearranged, with a bass line underneath at half the speed, as slow and heavy as dub. It was spread by pirate radio stations broadcasting from tower-block roofs, and by tapes of the DJs' sets, with MCs chatting over the top in the way of the sound systems.

The most famous break of all is about six seconds long: the drum solo in "Amen, Brother", the B-side of a 1969 single by a soul band called the Winstons, played by their drummer Gregory Coleman. Jungle producers used it so often that it became the sound of the music; it has since been sampled on thousands of records, in jungle, hip-hop, pop and adverts. Coleman was never paid for it, and died homeless in 2006. Remember the box in section 6.1: a sample is someone's work.

In 1994 jungle reached the charts: Shy FX and UK Apachi's "Original Nuttah", and M-Beat and General Levy's "Incredible", which got into the top ten. Goldie, a graffiti artist from the West Midlands, started the Metalheadz label that year with the DJs Kemistry and Storm, and his album Timeless (1995) showed jungle could be long, orchestral and sad as well as fierce. DJ Rap was one of the scene's first star DJs, and LTJ Bukem made it smooth and spacious, close to the ambient of chapter 7. In 1997 Roni Size and Reprazent's New Forms, from Bristol, won the Mercury Prize.

By the late 1990s the music was mostly called drum and bass, and it had tightened up: cleaner drums, often the "two-step", a kick and snare pattern you'll build in Track 3, at 170 to 176, and darker, heavier basses. The favourite of those came from Detroit: Kevin Saunderson, one of the techno pioneers of chapter 3, recording as Reese in 1988, made a bass of two slightly detuned sawtooth waves beating against each other, and drum and bass producers took it, and its name, as their own. Drum and bass is still everywhere: in clubs, at festivals, in pop records, and in its own endless offshoots.

8.2 What jungle is made of

  • ·The tempo. Fast: 160 to 176. These tracks are at 170 and 172.
  • ·A break, sped up. Faster and higher, cut up and rearranged: the "edit".
  • ·A bass at half speed. The drums run at 170, the bass moves as if the tempo were 85, the speed of dub and reggae. Your head follows the drums; your body follows the bass.
  • ·Sub bass. So low it's felt more than heard, from the reggae sound systems.
  • ·Fills and edits at the end of every phrase, eight bars at a time, as in techno, but far busier.
  • ·Echo throws. A single moment sent into an echo, from dub.

As with hip-hop, a lot of jungle was made to be played with an MC on top, chatting and toasting in the sound-system style. That's theirs, and as in chapter 6 we'll stay behind the decks.

8.3 Track 1 at a glance

Jungle Track 1 is Taste's break turned up to 170 and chopped, two bars of it rearranged, an 808 kick underneath, and a half-time sub bass on Volt.

Sound 8.1  Jungle Track 1, as built in sections 8.5 to 8.8: the break turned up ten semitones to 170 and chopped, two bars of it rearranged, an 808 kick under it and a half-time sub.

8.4 Speeding up a break

In chapter 6, chopping let the break play at a new tempo without changing its pitch. Jungle did it the other way, on purpose. On the old samplers, the simple way to make a break faster was to play it higher, like a record at the wrong speed, and jungle's producers loved what that did: the drums got faster, tighter and higher, with a snap that playing them faster any other way doesn't give. So that's what you'll do.

Taste's starter break was played at 95. Every semitone up plays it about 6% faster; twelve, an octave, plays it at twice the speed. Ten semitones up is 1.78 times as fast: 95 times 1.78 is 169, just about the 170 of this track. Then CHOP cuts it into sixteen slices, so Step can rearrange it.

8.5 Setting up

A new song, and a break of your own

  • 1Join the units in this order from the Root: Step, Taste, Strike, Volt, Haze.
  • 2On STEP, SONG›4ACTION›NEW›hold4, and name it. Then TEMPO›1TEMPO›170, and leave Step on TEMPO while you set up Taste.
  • 3On TASTE, SOUNDS›1BANK›FAC A›2SOUND›BREAK SYNC.
  • 4You're about to change it, so make it a sound of your own first. Turn encoder 3, COPY TO, to an empty slot, one that says INIT SOUND, and hold3.

Copying over a sound you made

COPY TO stays on the last slot it copied to. If you made the hip-hop tracks, it's still on USER A 01, which holds your gritty break, and copying there would replace it. Turn it on to USER A 02, or any slot that says INIT SOUND.

Why Step stays on TEMPO

While Step is on ENTRY, every key you press on another unit is written into Step's open track. Setting up Taste means pressing its keys to choose which slice to change, so keep Step on another page, TEMPO or SONG, until the setting up is done.

Faster, and chopped

  • 1On TASTE, press C3: BREAK SYNC has the whole bar there.
  • 2Press TUNE. Turn encoder 3, BEATS, right down to OFF (BREAK SYNC had it fitted to the tempo), then encoder 1, COARSE, up to +10.
  • 3Press CHOP. It opens on SLICES 16 and MODE EVENLY: hold4.

Press C3 to D#4 slowly in turn: the sixteen slices of a break that's a whole bar at 170. Each slice also keeps BREAK SYNC's choke, "one key at a time", so each one cuts off the one before; when Step rearranges them, no slice rings on over the next and smudges the beat.

The kit, the sub and three tracks

  • 1On STRIKE, BOOM.
  • 2On VOLT, SOUNDS›1BANK›FAC A›2SOUND›SUB BASS. No OCT this time: SUB BASS already sounds two octaves below the keys.
  • 3On STEP, on TRACKS: track 1 TASTE, LOOP 2 BARS; track 2 STRIKE, LOOP 1 BAR; track 3 VOLT, LOOP AUTO.

8.6 The edit, the kick and the sub

Two bars of break

On STEP, ENTRY, LENGTH 1/16, BAR at 1. On TASTE, bar 1 is the break as it was played: C3, C#3, D3 and on up every key, black and white, to D#4. Then carry on into bar 2, the edit:

Bar 2, beat 1C3C#3D3D#3
Beat 2E3F3F#3D#3
Beat 3D3D#3A#3B3
Beat 4C4D#4E3G3

The first half is the break as it was; then the kick (D#3 is slice 4, a kick) comes early, twice, pushing beat 3 off balance, and the bar ends snare, ghost, snare, ghost, tumbling into bar 1. A bar as played and a bar cut up, round and round: that's the pattern of a lot of jungle.

The kick

Track 2, LENGTH 1/16, BAR at 1, on STRIKE: KICK, nine rests, KICK, five rests: under the break's own kicks on beat 1 and the "and" of beat 3, as in hip-hop, for the weight a small, fast break hasn't got.

The sub, at half speed

Track 3, BAR at 1, on VOLT, four bars, each a minim (LENGTH 1/2) then a crotchet rest and a crotchet (LENGTH 1/4):

Bar1/21/41/4
1G3restF3
2G3restA#3
3D#3restD3
4F3restG3

Two notes a bar, while the break plays sixteen: the bass is moving at a quarter of the drums' speed, and that gap is jungle's whole feeling of speed and stillness at once. The notes are from G minor, and the line leans on the bottom note, G, the way dub basses do. You'll hear the G at G1, about 49 vibrations a second, nearly at the bottom of what you can hear: on small speakers it almost disappears, which is why jungle sounds so different on a big sound system.

8.7 Balance, and remembering

On STEP, MIXER: TASTE 0, STRIKE -6, VOLT up to +3. Jungle is a music for big speakers, and its sub sits louder than its drums. Then SONG›4ACTION›REMEMBER SOUNDS›hold4: it remembers your copy of the break, so your changes come back with the song.

On TRACKS, mute tracks 2 and 3, and press PLAY.

BarsAs it starts
1-8The break alone.
9-16Unmute track 2: the kick.
17-32Unmute track 3: the sub.
33-40Mute tracks 1 and 2: the sub alone. The floor drops away.

At 170 a bar goes by in under a second and a half, so eight bars is about eleven seconds: count in phrases, not bars, and watch Step's bar number.

Try this

Write your own edit in bar 2. Try COARSE +12 on Taste, an octave up, for a break at 190 that sounds tiny and frantic, and lower the tempo to match it, or not. Try a sub line of your own, one or two notes a bar, from G minor's scale: G, A, A#, C, D, D#, F.

Jungle Track 2 is Track 1 with the tricks: two new sounds made from slices, a backwards snare and a lower one, in a four-bar break with a fill; a crash every eight bars; and the break thrown into Haze's echo at the end of every phrase.

8.10 Setting up

On STEP, load jungle Track 1, then SONG›4ACTION›DUPLICATE›hold4, and name the copy. On TRACKS, unmute any track that says MUTED, then come back to SONG, so Step isn't on ENTRY while you work on Taste.

8.11 New sounds from old slices

CHOP's third MODE, COPY, copies one key, with its slice and all its settings, onto another, so you can change the copy and keep the original.

  • 1On TASTE, press CHOP, and turn encoder 2, MODE, one click, then another: from EVENLY to AT HITS to COPY. It moves one choice a turn, so turn it a click at a time.
  • 2Press C4, slice 13, the snare on beat 3. Turn encoder 1, TO, to E4, the first key above the slices, and hold4.
  • 3On E4, press TRIM and turn encoder 3, REVERSE, to ON: the snare backwards, a swell that sucks up into nothing.
  • 4Press E3, slice 5, the snare on beat 2. On CHOP (still on COPY), TO to F4, and hold4.
  • 5On F4, press TUNE and turn COARSE down 5, from +10 to +5: a deeper, slower snare.

Look before you hold

Holding encoder 4 on CHOP does whatever MODE says. If it says EVENLY or AT HITS, it chops the key you're on into slices across the keys above it, replacing what was there. Make sure the screen says COPY before you hold.

8.12 A four-bar break, a crash, and throws

The break, with a fill

On STEP, on TRACKS, track 1: LOOP up to 4 BARS, then hold4 to clear it. On ENTRY, BAR to 1, LENGTH 1/16, and on TASTE write bars 1 and 2 as in Track 1, bar 3 the break as played (C3 to D#4 again), and bar 4 the fill:

Bar 4, beat 1C3C#3D3D#3
Beat 2E3D#4F#3D#3
Beat 3F4G3E3F4
Beat 4E3E3E3E4

The low snare (F4) thumps under beat 3, the snare rolls in semiquavers through beat 4, and the very last note is the backwards snare, swelling into the first beat of the next four bars. Four bars round, the break tells you where you are: three bars that keep time, and a fourth that throws you into the next.

A crash every eight bars

On TRACKS, track 4: give it STRIKE and turn LOOP up to 8 BARS. On ENTRY, BAR to 1, and press CRASH once. A loop eight bars long with one note in it: a crash on the first beat of every phrase. Step's tracks can loop over 1, 2, 4 and 8 bars all at once, each going round on its own.

The echo, and throwing into it

  • 1On HAZE, press the 6th white key from the top: DUB ECHO.
  • 2SENDS, and turn TASTE, STRIKE and VOLT all right down to 0. Nothing goes into the echo, for now.
  • 3On STEP, SONG›4ACTION›REMEMBER SOUNDS›hold4.

A throw is a trick from dub reggae, where the engineer played the mixing desk like an instrument: send one moment, a snare or a word, into the echo, and take it straight out again, so only that moment repeats, trailing away into the distance while the music goes on. You'll throw the last bar of every phrase.

On TRACKS, mute tracks 2 and 3, and press PLAY. Keep Haze's SENDS page in reach.

17-32Unmute track 3: the sub.

Try this

Throw something else: Strike's send, on one snare. Make more sounds from slices: a kick tuned down a whole octave, a hat reversed. Try the crash on a 6-bar loop, so it lands somewhere different in every phrase.

8.14 Track 3: your own

Duplicate Track 2 and make it yours: the tempo, the edits and fills, the sub line, the throws. Section 8.16 has one way it might go: drum and bass, using the changes in section 8.15. Every jungle producer worth hearing cut up the break their own way, and that's the part we can't write down for you.

8.15 Drum and bass

Faster, a two-step, and a bass that growls

  • 1On STEP, TEMPO›1TEMPO›172.
  • 2On STRIKE, PUNCH: a tighter kick.
  • 3On VOLT, SOUNDS›1BANK›FAC A›2SOUND›GROWL, then press FILTER, ready for later.
  • 4GROWL sits an octave above SUB BASS, so move the bass down an octave: on TRACKS, track 3; on ENTRY, BAR to 1, COPY, push encoder 1 for TRANSPOSE, turn END on 12 beats (to the end of bar 4), SEMITONES to -12, and hold4.
  • 5On TRACKS, track 5: STRIKE, LOOP 1 BAR. On ENTRY, BAR to 1, LENGTH 1/4, and on STRIKE: rest, SNARE, rest, SNARE.
  • 6On STEP, MIXER: TASTE down to -6, STRIKE up to 0, VOLT down to -9.
  • 7SONG›4ACTION›REMEMBER SOUNDS›hold4.

Track 2's kick on beat 1 and the "and" of 3, and track 5's snare on 2 and 4: that's the two-step, the backbone of drum and bass, clean and hard. The break, turned down, rides on top as a shuffle, filling the gaps. And GROWL is Volt's take on the Reese: three oscillators slightly out of tune with each other, beating and churning.

A big bass takes a lot of room

GROWL is loud in a way SUB BASS isn't: its sound is in the middle of the range, where the ear is most sensitive, as well as at the bottom, and a wide, detuned sound fills the whole space. At VOLT 0 it swallows the drums. At -9 it sits just under them. Drum and bass mixes are a fight between the drums and the bass, and the drums have to win.

8.17 What you've learned

  • ·Where jungle and drum and bass came from: rave, the sound systems, pirate radio, the Amen break and the man who played it.
  • ·Speeding a break up by playing it higher, and what semitones do to speed.
  • ·Keeping your own copy of a sound, and not copying over another.
  • ·The edit and the fill; a half-time bass under double-time drums; sub bass.
  • ·New sounds from slices: CHOP's COPY, REVERSE, re-tuning.
  • ·Loops of 1, 2, 4 and 8 bars at once; transposing by an octave.
  • ·Echo throws, played live.
  • ·The two-step and the Reese bass, and why the drums have to win.

Next, synth-pop and synthwave: the whole range at once, chords, arpeggios and a tune, and a song written out from beginning to end.

Chapter 9 - Synth-pop and synthwave

Chords that move, an octave bass, an arpeggio, a tune, and a key change.

Every chapter so far has kept away from one thing: a tune. Techno threw out the chord progression, house looped two chords, hip-hop left the space for a voice, ambient let the harmony drift. Synth-pop is pop music: it has a progression that goes somewhere and comes back, and a melody you can sing. This chapter builds one section of a pop song, its chords, its band and its tune, eight bars that go round; a whole song, with verses, a chorus, a bridge and an ending, is the next step, and section 12.3 points the way. It's also the one chapter that needs almost the whole range at once.

What you need for this chapter

The Root, Step, Strike, Volt, Ember and Haze, joined in that order, and headphones. Track 2 adds Glass and Axis on the end. That's seven units on one Root.

9.1 Where synth-pop and synthwave came from

Chapter 2 told how Kraftwerk and Giorgio Moroder made pop records from machines in the 1970s. At the end of the decade, cheaper synthesisers put that sound in the hands of bands. In Tokyo, Yellow Magic Orchestra, formed in 1978, had hits with synthesisers and sequencers; in 1979 Gary Numan, with Tubeway Army, took "Are 'Friends' Electric?" to number one in Britain with a sound he'd found by accident on a Minimoog in the studio.

The early 1980s were synth-pop's golden years, and much of it came from British bedrooms and art schools. The Human League's "Don't You Want Me" was the Christmas number one of 1981; Soft Cell's "Tainted Love" and Depeche Mode's first records came the same year. Yazoo paired Vince Clarke's synthesisers with Alison Moyet's huge voice; Eurythmics' "Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This)" (1983) is Annie Lennox singing over a single sequenced bass line and a drum machine. Laurie Anderson's "O Superman" (1981), eight minutes of a looped "ha" and a vocoder, got to number two, and Kate Bush used one of the first sampling computers, the Fairlight, on her records from 1980. In 1983 New Order's "Blue Monday", built on a drum machine and sequencers, became the best-selling 12-inch single ever made in Britain. Then the Yamaha DX7, and Roland's Juno synthesisers, put the sound on nearly every pop record of the decade.

By the 1990s that sound was out of fashion, which, as with the 808, is exactly when people started to love it again. In the 2000s, producers who'd grown up on 80s film scores, John Carpenter's in particular, and on video games, made new music in the old style, and called it synthwave or retrowave: Kavinsky's "Nightcall" (2010), in the film Drive (2011), made it famous. Kyle Dixon and Michael Stein's theme for the television series Stranger Things (2016) is played entirely on analogue synthesisers, and in 2019 the Weeknd's "Blinding Lights", all octave bass and 80s drums, became one of the most-played songs there has ever been. Bands such as Chvrches, with Lauren Mayberry's voice over the synths, brought synth-pop itself back.

9.2 What synth-pop is made of

  • ·The tempo. Pop speed: about 100 to 120. These tracks are at 112 and 116.
  • ·Pop drums. A kick on 1 and 3 and a snare on 2 and 4, the backbeat of rock and pop, rather than four to the floor; the snare huge and echoing. In the 80s that sound was gated reverb, a big reverb cut off dead; Haze has no gate, so its BIG HALL stands in.
  • ·The octave bass, a note and the same note an octave up, on every quaver, from disco and Moroder's "I Feel Love".
  • ·Pads: soft, wide chords, held.
  • ·Arpeggios: the chords played a note at a time, fast and even, as only a machine can.
  • ·A tune on a lead synth, and a song's shape: verses and choruses, a breakdown, and a big finish.

Four chords

All three tracks are in A minor on four chords, a bar each: A minor, F, C, G. In Roman numerals, as in house, that's i, VI, III, VII. Now count the same four chords in C major instead: C is I, so A minor is vi, F is IV and G is V: vi, IV, I, V. A minor and C major share all their notes, and are called each other's relative minor and major; the same four chords, started on C (C, G, A minor, F, or C, A minor, F, G), are the chords of thousands of pop songs, from "Let It Be" to the present. Starting on A minor gives them the shadow synthwave loves, a sound halfway between sad and heroic.

9.3 Track 1 at a glance

Synthwave Track 1 is the band: pop drums on Strike, an octave bass on Volt, the four chords on an Ember pad, and Haze's big hall. Nothing new on Step: everything comes from earlier chapters.

9.8 Track 2 at a glance

Synthwave Track 2 adds the two things that make it unmistakably 80s: an arpeggio on Glass, played by Step's arpeggiator from the same four chords, and an eight-bar tune on Axis.

Sound 9.2  Synthwave Track 2, as built in sections 9.9 to 9.13: the band, an arpeggio on Glass from Step's arpeggiator, and an eight-bar tune on Axis.

9.9 Setting up

  • 1On STEP, load synthwave Track 1, then SONG›4ACTION›DUPLICATE›hold4, and name the copy. On TRACKS, unmute any track that says MUTED.
  • 2Join Glass, then Axis, to the right-hand end of the row.
  • 3On GLASS, SOUNDS›1BANK›FAC A›2SOUND›E.PIANO 1.
  • 4On AXIS, SOUNDS›1BANK›FAC A›2SOUND›SYNC LEAD.

A gentler lead, and a sound of your own

SYNC LEAD is a classic lead: one voice at a time, sliding from note to note, and very bright, especially as each note starts. Make it smoother and softer:

  • 1On AXIS, press KEYS and turn encoder 3, GLIDE, down 10 clicks, from 30 to 20: a quicker slide between notes.
  • 2Press FILTER and turn encoder 1, CUTOFF, down 12 clicks, from 70 to 58: darker.
  • 3Keep it: SOUNDS, turn encoder 3, COPY TO, to an empty slot that says INIT SOUND, and hold3. (If you made ambient Track 3, USER A 01 is your AIR PAD: use USER A 02.)
  • 4Press Axis's OCT+ once: the tune sits an octave up.

Seven tracks

On TRACKS: tracks 4 and 5, the bass and the chords, LOOP 4 BARS; track 6, GLASS, LOOP 4 BARS; track 7, AXIS, left on AUTO.

Why set loops on tracks that were fine on AUTO? Because the tune is going to be eight bars long. AUTO tracks together make up the song, and the song lasts as long as the longest of them, whole bars, playing each AUTO track once each time round. With the tune at eight bars, a four-bar AUTO bass would play bars 1 to 4 and then stop for 5 to 8. Given a loop of its own, it goes round twice while the tune goes round once.

9.10 The arpeggio

An arpeggio is a chord played one note at a time. Step has an arpeggiator on every track: give it chords and it plays them as arpeggios, so you don't write the notes at all.

  • 1The chords first. On TRACKS, turn to track 5; on ENTRY, BAR to 1, and press COPY. Turn END on 12 beats, to the end of bar 4. Turn encoder 1, TO, on one, to track 6, and encoder 2 back to bar 1. hold4.
  • 2On TRACKS, turn to track 6, then press TRACKS again: the top bar says ARP.
  • 3Turn encoder 1, PATTERN, on one, from OFF to UP, and encoder 3, OCTAVES, on one, to 2. Leave RATE at 1/16 and GATE at 50%. Press TRACKS to go back.

Track 6 has the same four chords as track 5, a whole bar each, but now Step plays each one going up, a semiquaver a note, over two octaves, then starting again, and GATE holds each note for half its time, so they bounce. Ember holds the chords; Glass ripples through them. Chords stay chords on every other track: the arpeggiator belongs to track 6 alone.

9.11 The tune

On TRACKS, turn to track 7; on ENTRY, BAR to 1, and press LEGATO, the third button in Step's left column, so every note lasts right up to the next. On a lead that glides, that's what makes it slide from note to note instead of starting each one afresh. Then on AXIS, eight bars:

BarChordNotes (LENGTH)
1AmA4 (1/2), C5 (1/4), B4 (1/4)
2FA4, F4, A4, C5 (1/4 each)
3CG4 (1/2), E4 (1/4), G4 (1/4)
4GD5 (1/2), B4 (1/2)
5AmC5 (1/4), B4 (1/8), A4 (1/8), B4 (1/4), C5 (1/4)
6FA4 (1/2), F4 (1/4), C5 (1/4)
7CG4, E4, G4, C5 (1/4 each)
8GB4 (1/2), rest (1/2)

Then press NORMAL again, so the next notes you write anywhere aren't legato too.

Look at the first note of every bar: A over A minor, A over F, G over C, D over G. Each is a note of the chord underneath (A minor is A, C, E; F is F, A, C; C is C, E, G; G is G, B, D). A tune that lands on the chord's notes on the strong beats sounds as if it belongs with the chords; the notes in between can wander, and the B over A minor in bar 1 rubs for a moment before the next bar puts it right. The tune is two halves of four bars, the second answering the first, and it ends on a breath, a minim of rest, before it starts again: a melody needs somewhere to breathe, like the singer it stands in for.

9.12 The hall, and the mix

  • 1On HAZE, still on SENDS from Track 1, the fourth box is now GLASS: turn it to 30.
  • 2Press SENDS again: the top bar says SENDS 5-8, the units after the first four. Turn AXIS to 40.
  • 3On STEP, MIXER: EMBER up 3, to -10. Then press MIXER again for units 5 to 8: GLASS down to -13, AXIS up to +1.
  • 4SONG›4ACTION›REMEMBER SOUNDS›hold4.

Pressing a page again

With more than four units, Haze's SENDS and Step's MIXER each have two pages, and pressing the button again turns between them. So before you turn anything, look at the top bar: if Haze already shows SENDS, pressing SENDS again takes you to SENDS 5-8, not back to the start.

9.13 Playing Track 2

On TRACKS, mute tracks 1, 2, 3, 4 and 7, so the pad and the arpeggio start alone, and press PLAY.

BarsAs it starts
1-8The pad and the arpeggio.
9-16Unmute tracks 1, 3 and 4: the kick, the hats and the bass.
17-32Unmute tracks 2 and 7: the snare, and the tune.
33-40Mute tracks 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6: the breakdown, the pad and the tune alone.
41-56Unmute tracks 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6: everything.
57-64Mute tracks 1, 2, 3, 4 and 7: the pad and the arpeggio, as it began. STOP at the end of bar 64.

Try this

On track 6's ARP page, try the other PATTERNs, RATE 1/8, OCTAVES 3, a shorter GATE. Try the arpeggio on Glass's HARPSICH 1 or SYN-CLAV 1, and the tune on Axis's HOLLOWLEAD. Write your own tune over the same chords: start every bar on one of the chord's notes, and see where it wants to go.

9.14 Track 3: your own

This is the last of the third tracks, and the last time we'll say it: what follows is one way it might go, about the plainest synth-pop we could build, so that the method shows through. It isn't a song yet: it's one eight-bar section, the same chords and tune all the way through, with no verse, no chorus of its own, no bridge and no real ending. What you write over these chords, or over chords of your own, with your own tune, and a chorus to go with it, will be better than ours, and it should sound nothing like it.

Synthwave Track 3 is Track 2 written out bar by bar, as house Track 3 was, so that it plays itself; a little faster; and with one thing that only a written-out song can have: the last sixteen bars go up a key.

9.15 Writing it out, and a key change

  • 1On STEP, load synthwave Track 2, then SONG›4ACTION›DUPLICATE›hold4, and name the copy. Unmute any track that says MUTED.
  • 2TEMPO›1TEMPO›116.

Eight bars of everything

As in house Track 3 (section 5.15), make every track an ordinary AUTO track the length of the song. For tracks 1 to 6: on TRACKS, turn LOOP right down to AUTO; on ENTRY, BAR to 1, COPY (for tracks 4, 5 and 6, turn END on 12 beats, to the end of bar 4: their four bars); push encoder 1 three times, to FILL; turn UNTIL right up, and hold2. UNTIL stops at 8:4.1: the song is eight bars long, set by the tune, and FILL won't go past it.

Sixty-four bars, carved

Then, as in house: SONG, SONG again for SECTIONS; END on 7 bars, to bar 8; push encoder 1 three times, to FILL; UNTIL to 64:1.1, and hold2. Now carve the arrangement out with DELETE (section 5.15 has the method: COPY, push encoder 1 twice, END first, then START, hold4):

TrackBarsEND onSTART onWhy
1 kick, 3 hats, 4 bass1-828 beats0The intro: the pad and the arpeggio
2 snare, 7 tune1-1660 beats0
1, 2, 3, 4, and 6 arpeggio33-40156 beats128 beatsThe breakdown: the pad and the tune

Up a semitone

For tracks 4, 5, 6 and 7, the bass, the chords, the arpeggio and the tune: on ENTRY, BAR to 1, COPY, push encoder 1 for TRANSPOSE, turn END on to 64:4.1 and then START on to 49:1.1 (they turn faster the quicker you turn them), SEMITONES to +1, and hold4. The drums stay as they are: they have no key.

From bar 49 the whole song is in B flat minor instead of A minor, a semitone higher. In a pop song it's the oldest trick there is for the last chorus: everything you already know, suddenly lifted, as if the song had taken a breath and stood up. Here there's no chorus to lift, so it lifts the one section there is, but the effect is the same. It was so common in 80s pop that it got a nickname, the "truck driver's gear change". A semitone is the most obvious lift there is: nearly every note of the old key moves, so you can't miss it. It's also a thing you can only do by writing a song out: a loop is the same every time round, but a written-out song can change in its last sixteen bars and stay changed.

9.16 One way it might go

Sound 9.3  Synthwave Track 3, one way it might go: Track 2 written out bar by bar at 116, so it plays itself, and from bar 49 everything but the drums a semitone higher.

Press PLAY and listen for two things. The arrangement plays itself, as house Track 3 did. And at bar 49, a little under two minutes in, everything but the drums moves up a semitone: the tune you've heard four times comes round again and sounds new.

9.17 What you've learned

  • ·Where synth-pop and synthwave came from, from YMO and Gary Numan to "Blinding Lights".
  • ·Pop drums, the octave bass, and a big hall on the snare.
  • ·The four chords, relative major and minor, and why the same chords sound different starting somewhere else.
  • ·Step's arpeggiator: chords played a note at a time.
  • ·A tune: chord notes on the strong beats, two halves that answer each other, room to breathe; LEGATO and glide.
  • ·Why a short track needs a set loop under a longer AUTO one.
  • ·SENDS and MIXER for units 5 to 8.
  • ·A key change, and why only a written-out song can have one.

That's the last of the kinds of music. You've made seven, and by now you know the tools well enough to make an eighth that has no name yet.

Chapter 10 - Step from start to finish

Every page and every button, in order, with where in the book you'll use each one.

The chapters of music teach Step a piece at a time, as each kind of music needs it. This chapter is the other way round: the whole of Step, page by page, with nothing left out. If you've read the chapters before it, it fills in the gaps and puts everything in one place. If you've come here first, it's a map: read it through once, then go to chapter 3 and start making music, and come back whenever you want to know what something does.

What you need for this chapter

The Root and Step, with any one unit that makes a sound joined to its right, so you can hear what you write. Volt or Glass is ideal.

10.1 What Step is

Step doesn't make any sound of its own. It holds notes, and sends them to the other units at the right moments, along the chain. Everything it holds is on one timeline: bars and beats, one after another, like a score, from bar 1 to the end of the song. There are no "patterns" to switch between and no grid of steps that goes round: a note is simply at its place, bar 13 beat 2, on its track.

A song has 16 tracks. Each track plays one unit, and several tracks can play the same unit: in techno Track 1, the kick, the hats and the clap are three tracks all playing Strike. Every track shares the same timeline, so bar 13 is bar 13 on all of them. A song has room for 8,192 notes, shared by all sixteen tracks, and Step keeps up to 32 songs, saving as you go.

You write notes in step time: you choose how long a note is, play it, and the cursor moves on by that much. Nothing depends on playing in time, so you can take as long as you like over every note.

10.2 The layout

Step's buttons are arranged by what they affect, from small to large:

  • The left column (1): the note you're writing: how much of its length it sounds (STACC, NORMAL, LEGATO), whether it's ACCENTed or SLIDes into the next, and DOTTED to make it half as long again.
  • The middle column (2): one track: ENTRY to write notes, CHORD to write chords by name, COPY to copy, transpose, delete and fill, and TRACKS for the track's own settings.
  • The right column (3): the whole song: PLAY and STOP, MIXER, TEMPO, SONG, and SETUP at the bottom, as on every unit.

Step's keys play notes on the open track's unit, so you can write with them. Their lights show one bar of the open track: a white key is dim where a note starts, bright at the cursor and blinking as it plays, sixteenths across the bar; the black keys count which bar it is. OCT- and OCT+ move Step's keys, and the CHORD page's chords, by octaves.

10.3 ENTRY: writing notes

ENTRY is where notes are written into the open track. Play a note, or a chord, and it goes in at the cursor with the current length; when every key is let go, the cursor moves on by that length.

EncoderTurnPushHold
1 LENGTHThe note's length: 1/16T, 1/16, 1/8T, 1/8, 1/4T, 1/4, 1/2T, 1/2, 1A rest of that lengthA tie: the note before carries on
2 PITCHThe note shown (or, with a note at the cursor, moves it)Writes the note shown
3 VELOHow hard: 1 to 127
4 BARMoves the cursor, a LENGTH at a timeINSERT or REPLACEDeletes the note at the cursor
  • Lengths are written as fractions of a bar of four beats: 1/4 is a crotchet (a quarter note), 1/8 a quaver, 1/16 a semiquaver, 1/2 a minim, 1 a semibreve, a whole bar. A T is a triplet: three in the time of two. Triplets can go anywhere, singly or in any number (chapter 3, section 3.2, has the counting).
  • Where notes come from. Step's own keys; the keys of the unit the track plays, at Step's VELO (chapter 3); a MIDI keyboard on Step's channel, at the strength you play; or a push of PITCH. Playing the keys of a different unit switches to that unit's track instead (the screen says which, and that first note isn't written), so on ENTRY, set up other units only on another of Step's pages: chapter 8 explains why.
  • INSERT and REPLACE. In INSERT, a new note goes in at the cursor and pushes everything after it along; in REPLACE it writes over whatever starts there. At the end of a track, both just add.
  • The cursor stays where you left it when you change track: turn BAR back to the start before writing a new part (chapter 3).

10.4 The note's shape

  • STACC, NORMAL, LEGATO, one of the three: a note sounds for a short part of its length, most of it, or all of it, right up to the next. LEGATO is how a gliding lead slides from note to note (chapter 9).
  • ACCENT: the note is played harder; on Volt's ACID sounds, it's the original's accent (chapter 4). Strike's ACCENT setting says how much louder.
  • SLIDE: the note glides into the next; Volt's ACID sounds slide as the original does (chapter 4).
  • DOTTED: the length half as long again: a dotted crotchet is three quavers long.

Whatever is lit applies to the next note you write, and the lights show the note at the cursor. They work only on ENTRY and CHORD. To add an accent or a slide to a note already written, move BAR onto it and press the button.

10.5 CHORD: chords by name

Choose a chord by name and Step works out its notes. Chapter 5 teaches it.

EncoderTurnPush
1The ROOT (C to B) or the TYPE (major, m, 7, maj7, m7, dim7, m7b5, aug, sus2, sus4, 6, m6, add9, 7sus4), whichever is underlinedSwitches between ROOT and TYPE
2 INVERTRoot position, 1ST, 2ND, 3RD: the chord turned over
3 LENGTHAs on ENTRY
4 BARMoves the cursorPlaces the chord; the cursor moves on by its length

Every chord is four notes: a three-note chord adds its lowest note again, an octave up. The screen spells the notes as the chord is written (A flat minor is Ab, Cb, Eb), and the chord plays on the track's unit as you change it. Chords start at C3; OCT- and OCT+ move them.

10.6 COPY: copy, transpose, delete and fill

COPY works on a range of the open track, from the start of START's beat to the end of END's beat. It opens on the cursor's bar, always in COPY mode. Push encoder 1 to step through the four jobs; hold any encoder to do it (with the bar filling); the screen says what was done.

ModeEncoder 1Encoder 2What it doesWhere it's taught
COPYThe track to copy toTO: where the copy startsCopies the range, replacing whatever is there3.5
TRANSPOSESEMITONES, -12 to +12Moves the range's notes up or down3.5
DELETERemoves the range's notes, leaving silence5.15
FILLHow many times (shown)UNTIL: the last beat filledRepeats the range after itself, up to UNTIL5.15

Encoders 3 and 4 are START and END. Positions move a beat a click; push encoder 2, 3 or 4 to move them in sixteenths instead. Turn END before START: START can't pass it.

10.7 TRACKS, and how tracks loop

TRACKS is each track's own settings.

EncoderTurnPushHold
1 TRACKWhich trackMutes it, or unmutes it
2 UNITWhich unit it plays
3 LOOPAUTO, or a set loop in barsThe loop in beats instead
4 NOTES(shows how many)Clears the track
  • Muting keeps the track's notes and stops it playing: the way to arrange live (chapter 3).
  • A track can play any unit, and can be moved to another at any time; its notes stay (chapter 7). If a track's unit isn't on the chain, the track shows it's missing, keeps everything, and plays again when the unit comes back.
  • Hold TRACKS on any page, turn encoder 1 to another track, and let go: you're back on the page you were on, on the new track.
  • TRACKS pressed again is the track's arpeggiator, ARP: PATTERN (OFF, UP, DOWN, UP/DN, PLAYED, RANDOM), RATE, OCTAVES and GATE (chapter 9). Chords stay stored as chords; the arpeggio is how they're played.

AUTO and set loops

This is the one idea about Step that's worth reading twice.

  • AUTO tracks make the song. The song is as long as its longest AUTO track, in whole bars, and every AUTO track plays its notes once each time the song goes round, then is silent until the song starts again. So AUTO tracks always stay in step with each other. A four-bar AUTO track in an eight-bar song plays for four bars and rests for four (chapter 9).
  • A set loop runs on its own. A track with a LOOP of 1 BAR, or 3 beats, or 17, repeats every so many beats from PLAY, whatever the song does, and never starts again with it. That's how a one-bar drum pattern lasts the whole song (chapter 3), how three beats go round against four (chapter 4), and how five loops never line up (chapter 7).
  • With no AUTO track holding notes, the song is as long as its longest set loop.

10.8 PLAY, STOP, and MIXER

PLAY always starts the song from the top, and STOP stops it. Pressing PLAY also sends each unit to the sound the song remembers (SONG's REMEMBER SOUNDS, below), so any temporary changes to those sounds are dropped (chapter 6). As it plays, Step also sends MIDI clock, start and stop, and the Root can pass them out of its MIDI OUT (SETUP, ROOT, MIDI OUT: CLOCK or BOTH), so music software or another instrument can follow it.

MIXER has a level and a mute for each unit, four to a page, in the order they're joined: turn for the level, from OFF and -48 dB up to +6 dB; push to mute. With more than four units, MIXER pressed again shows the rest. The mix is kept with the song, so each song has its own. Haze's sends follow these levels: a unit turned down here is turned down in the echo and reverb too.

10.9 TEMPO: tempo, swing and time signature

EncoderTurnPush
1 TEMPOBeats a minute, 30 to 300
2The time signature's top number: beats in a bar
3 SWINGOFF (50%) to 75%Swings the semiquavers (1/16) or the quavers (1/8)
4The bottom number: which note is a beat (2, 4, 8 or 16)

Swing is chapter 5's: notes stay where they're written, and only the off-beat ones are played late.

The time signature is the one thing on Step that none of the chapters of music needed: every one of them is in 4/4, four crotchets to a bar, like almost all dance music. But plenty of music isn't. A waltz is 3/4, three crotchets a bar; "Take Five" by the Dave Brubeck Quartet is in 5/4; Pink Floyd's "Money" is in 7/4; and a lot of Balkan folk music is in 7/8, seven quavers to a bar, felt as groups of 2+2+3. Changing it changes what a bar is, everywhere on Step: BAR moves, the keys' lights, COPY's ranges, and LOOP's bars all count in the new bars.

Try this

Start a new song (SONG, NEW). On TEMPO, turn encoder 2 up to 7 and encoder 4 on to 8: 7/8. On ENTRY, LENGTH 1/8, write a bar of seven quavers on Strike: KICK, rest, SNARE, rest, KICK, rest, SNARE. Set the track's LOOP to 1 BAR and play it. It limps, and then it doesn't: count it 1-2, 1-2, 1-2-3 and you'll start to feel it. Then try 5/4.

10.10 SONG, and SECTIONS

EncoderTurnPush / hold
1 SONGBrowses the 32 songsPush: loads the one shown
2 NAMEThe letterPush: on to the next letter (up to 10)
3 LENGTH(shows the song's bars and notes)
4 ACTIONREMEMBER SOUNDS, NEW, DUPLICATE, DELETEHold: does it
  • REMEMBER SOUNDS asks every unit which sound it's playing and keeps the answers with the song; loading the song, or pressing PLAY, sends every unit back to its sound. It keeps which sound, not changes made to a factory sound, so keep a changed sound as a sound of your own first (chapters 6 and 7).
  • NEW starts an empty song; DUPLICATE carries on with a copy of this one, sounds and all (chapter 3); DELETE removes it.
  • ACTION stays where you left it. Turn it each time to the one you mean, and look before you hold: one turn past DUPLICATE is DELETE.
  • Songs save themselves as you work. There's no save button, and nothing is lost when you unsnap Step.

SECTIONS

SONG pressed again is SECTIONS: the COPY page's jobs, on every AUTO track at once, in whole bars (push encoder 2, 3 or 4 for beats). Encoder 1 chooses COPY, INSERT, DELETE or FILL; encoder 2 is TO (or UNTIL); encoders 3 and 4 are START and END. INSERT copies a section in and moves the rest of the song along; DELETE here closes the gap, unlike the COPY page's. Set-loop tracks are left alone, since they repeat by themselves. Chapter 5, section 5.15, builds a whole song with it.

10.11 SETUP

Step's SETUP is every unit's SETUP (chapter 1): THIS UNIT, with Step's MIDI channel, which is how a MIDI keyboard writes into Step, and its RESET page; and ROOT, with the Root's inputs, its MIDI OUT (which can carry Step's notes and clock to a computer or another instrument) and its MIDI IN.

10.12 Where each thing is taught

ChapterOn Step
3 TechnoNew songs, tracks and their units, ENTRY, lengths and rests, set loops of a bar, COPY and TRANSPOSE, MIXER, mutes, velocity, two-bar loops, DUPLICATE
4 AcidACCENT and SLIDE, a loop in beats against the bar
5 HouseCHORD, swing, REMEMBER SOUNDS, FILL, SECTIONS, DELETE: a song written out
6 Hip-hopWriting another unit's keys (a sampler's slices), two-bar loops with a fill, remembered sounds and user sounds
7 AmbientLoops of many lengths at once, clearing a track but keeping its loop, moving tracks to another unit
8 JungleLoops of 1, 2, 4 and 8 bars, transposing by an octave, keeping Step off ENTRY while setting up another unit
9 Synth-popThe arpeggiator, LEGATO, set loops under a longer AUTO track, MIXER for units 5 to 8, a key change
10The time signature

Next, the last chapter: taking it all out of the house, and playing it live.

Chapter 11 - Playing live

Your knobs from every unit on one box, your sounds a key away, and a set that's never played the same way twice.

Everything in this book can be played live. You've been doing it since chapter 3: every track mute at the right bar, every filter opened a click at a time, every echo thrown, was a performance, and no two of them were quite the same. This chapter is about doing that in front of people: preparing a set, keeping your hands on the few controls that matter, and Pilot, the unit made for it.

What you need for this chapter

Pilot, and the units of any chapter before this one. The examples use acid Track 3's: the Root, Step, Strike, Volt and Haze, with Pilot joined on the end. A chain takes eight units at most; with Step, Haze and Pilot, that leaves five for the sound.

11.1 Electronic music, live

Electronic musicians have always had to answer the question of what they're doing up there. Kraftwerk stood behind their consoles like engineers at a control desk, and made that the show. In the 1970s Suzanne Ciani gave concerts on a Buchla modular synthesiser, patching and playing it live. In the rave years a "live PA" meant the act's own machines on stage instead of a DJ's records: Orbital's set at Glastonbury in 1994, two brothers in head torches behind a wall of synthesisers and sequencers, is still talked about. Jeff Mills plays a TR-909 live inside his DJ sets, programming patterns on the fly; Daft Punk toured in 2006 and 2007 inside a lit-up pyramid, rebuilding their records live from their parts. They all do some version of what you've been doing: the music is mostly prepared, and the performance is in the choices, which part comes in when, how far a filter opens, when everything stops.

11.2 Pilot

Pilot makes no sound. It's a remote control for every other unit on the chain:

  • Fifteen knob pages (1), on the function buttons. Each page puts any four controls on its encoders, each from any unit: Volt's cutoff, Haze's echo, Step's tempo and a track mute, side by side.
  • LEARN (2), for filling a page: you turn the knob you want on the unit itself, and Pilot takes it.
  • Scenes (3), on the white keys: each key keeps which sound every unit is playing, and calls them all up at once.

Its encoders send "up three" or "down one", never a fixed value, so nothing jumps when you change page: each knob carries on from wherever its control already is. And its screen shows each control as its own unit shows it, in hertz, seconds or beats a minute.

11.3 A knob page

Load acid Track 3 on Step, and join Pilot to the end of the row. On VOLT, press SOUNDS, then ACID, so its ACID page is showing.

  • 1On PILOT, press PAGE 1, then LEARN. The screen says TURN A KNOB ON ANY UNIT, and the first box is outlined.
  • 2On VOLT, turn encoder 2, CUTOFF, one click. Pilot's first box fills with VOLT and ACID CUTOFF, and the outline moves on.
  • 3Turn Volt's encoder 3, RESONANCE, one click, then encoder 4, ENV MOD.
  • 4On STEP, press TEMPO and turn encoder 1 one click.
  • 5On PILOT, press LEARN again: done.

Now press PLAY on Step, and play acid Track 3 with your hands on Pilot alone: the three knobs that make acid what it is, and the tempo, on one box. Turn the tempo back where it was with Pilot's fourth encoder.

  • A box takes a control once, however far you turn the knob, then moves on, so turn each one just a click while learning.
  • To choose which box fills next, push its encoder while LEARN is on. To empty a box, hold its encoder until the bar fills.
  • Holding a page's button works as LEARN too, for as long as you hold it: quick for changing one box.
  • A box says MISSING when its unit isn't on the chain, and comes back when it is.

11.4 A page of mutes

Every arrangement in this book was made with track mutes on Step's TRACKS page: turn to the track, push. Live, that's two moves for every change, and the wrong track is one click away. Put them on Pilot instead:

  • 1On PILOT, press PAGE 2, then LEARN.
  • 2On STEP, press TRACKS. For tracks 1, 2, 3 and 4 in turn, turn encoder 1 to the track and push it twice: the first push teaches Pilot, the second puts the track back as it was.
  • 3On PILOT, press LEARN again.

Turn a Pilot encoder clockwise to mute its track, anticlockwise to bring it back. Now the kick, the hats, the clap and the line each have a knob of their own, and you can drop the kick out and bring it back without looking. Step's MIXER levels and mutes, and SWING, can go on a page the same way.

Try this

Make a page for Haze: on its SOURCE page, MIX, so you can ride the drive up through a breakdown as acid Track 3 does; and its echo's REPEATS. Make one for Strike: EDIT, a key, and the drum settings you'd like to play, an open hat's DECAY or the kick's TUNE. Give each page one job, and remember which is which: PAGE 1 the acid, PAGE 2 the mutes, PAGE 3 the effects.

11.5 Pilot's changes, and PLAY

Everything Pilot changes on a sound is a temporary edit, even on a sound of your own: the unit shows a star, and nothing you do in a set ever overwrites a sound you saved. That's what you want on stage, but it has one consequence worth knowing. When you press PLAY, Step sends every unit back to the sound the song remembers, and that drops every temporary edit. So press PLAY first, then play the knobs. If a song should start with a sound already changed, change it on the unit, keep it as a sound of your own, and remember that (chapter 6).

11.6 Scenes

A scene is which sound every unit is playing, kept on one of Pilot's white keys.

  • 1Choose a sound on every unit: say Strike on BOOM, Volt on ACID.
  • 2On PILOT, hold the first white key until the bar fills. Every unit's sound is kept there.
  • 3Choose other sounds: Strike on PUNCH, Volt on SQ SQUELCH. Hold the second white key.
  • 4Now press the first key, and then the second: all the units change at once.

The key of the scene last called up is lit, and keys with scenes are dim. A scene keeps which sound, like REMEMBER SOUNDS, not changes made to it: if a unit has temporary edits when you store, Pilot names it (VOLT 2: EDITED, NOT KEPT). Use scenes to change the whole band's sound in the middle of a song, on the first beat of a phrase, as if the record had changed.

11.7 Planning a set

  • Put the songs in order. Step keeps 32, by number. Name them, and play them in order down the list: between songs, STOP, turn SONG to the next, push to load it, and PLAY. A long echo or reverb on Haze rings on through the gap.
  • Remember every song's sounds, so loading a song puts every unit right, whatever you did to it in the song before.
  • Decide what you'll play by hand, and what plays itself. A song written out (chapter 5) plays the arrangement for you, and leaves your hands free for the knobs; a song of loops and mutes (chapter 3) gives you the arrangement to play. Most sets mix the two.
  • Practise the moves, the way you'd practise a piece on any instrument: the breakdown in acid Track 3 is eight bars of turning one knob at the right speed.
  • Know where the sound goes. PHONES and its volume wheel are for you; LINE OUT, at full level, goes to the mixer or the speakers, and into a computer to record the set.

And play your own songs, not ours. The book's tracks taught you the tools; the set is where nobody else can tell you what comes next.

11.8 What you've learned

  • ·That every track in the book was already a performance.
  • ·Pilot's knob pages, learned by turning the real knob; a page of track mutes.
  • ·Why Pilot's changes are temporary, and why to press PLAY before playing the knobs.
  • ·Scenes: a whole band's sounds on one key.
  • ·Planning a set: the songs in order, sounds remembered, what's played and what plays itself.

Last, where to go from here.

Chapter 12 - Where next

You know how tracks are made now. Here's where the road goes from here.

12.1 What you've learned

Seven kinds of music, three tracks each. You've built techno from four loops and a filter, made acid squelch, put chords and swing under house, chopped a break and your own voice for hip-hop, let chords drift past each other for ambient, sped a break up until it blurred, and written one section of a pop song out to the end, with a key change. On the way you've learned nearly everything Step does, and a good deal of music theory without ever sitting down to learn it.

And you've learned the craft the book's title promised. Go back to the introduction: underneath, a track is a few short parts going round, and what makes it music is what happens to them, what drops out and comes back, what builds, what's left out and when. You've done that in every chapter. Put on any electronic record now and you'll hear it being done.

12.2 Making Sounds

Every track in this book used the units' factory sounds, on purpose: so you could hear exactly what the book describes, and so the music, not the sound design, stayed the point. But you'll have noticed how often a track came alive when a sound changed: Taste's break going to twelve bits, Axis's pad turned darker, the lead given a quicker glide. Those were small turns of one or two knobs. Making Sounds, this book's companion, is about all the rest of them.

  • Your music will sound like you. Factory sounds are shared by everyone who owns the unit. A track built from sounds you made yourself sounds like nobody else's, and in electronic music the sound is half of the idea.
  • It's one unit at a time. Each chapter of Making Sounds takes one unit and builds a set of named sounds on it from scratch, so you learn the unit by making things on it, as this book taught Step.
  • It's the other half of the history. This book told you where the music came from; Making Sounds tells you where the sounds came from: FM and the bell-like sounds of the 1980s, the analogue filter, the drum machines, sampling, grains.
  • It works on everything. Filters, envelopes, operators and grains have the same names on every synthesiser there is. What you learn there, you keep, whatever you play next.

Making Sounds ends where this book begins, by pointing back here. Between them, you have both halves of electronic music: the sounds, and what to do with them.

12.3 There's plenty more music theory

Let's be honest about this book's theory. You've met a lot of it: crotchets and quavers, time signatures, semitones and octaves, scales and keys, chords and inversions, sevenths, voice leading, Roman numerals, relative minors, polyrhythm, a key change. That's a real foundation. It's also the beginning. Music theory is centuries deep, and the people who wrote the records you love mostly knew a great deal more of it than this, whether they learned it in a classroom or by ear. Here's some of what's next, and every bit of it will make you freer, never less free.

  • Song form. Synthwave Track 3 had one eight-bar progression all the way through. Real songs have verses, which tell the story, choruses, which come back with the hook and usually their own chords, a pre-chorus to lift into them, and a bridge (in Britain often the "middle eight"), a different passage before the last chorus so it lands fresh. Learn to hear where each starts in songs you know, then build them on Step with SECTIONS.
  • Harmony, and how chords move. Why does G to C sound like coming home? That pull, from the chord built on a key's fifth note back to its first, is a cadence, and there are several kinds, each a different way to end a phrase. Then there's the ii-V-I that runs through jazz, chords borrowed from the minor key into the major (and back), chromatic chords that slide a semitone, and key changes far stranger than chapter 9's.
  • Melody. Motifs, short ideas repeated and changed; call and response; tension and release; where a tune should climb and where it should rest; how the words of a song and its tune fit.
  • Rhythm. Syncopation, cross-rhythms from West African and Cuban music, the clave, odd time signatures that change from bar to bar.
  • Counterpoint: two or more tunes at once, each going its own way, fitting together, as in Bach.
  • Reading music. Written notation can look forbidding, but it's how most music of the last few centuries is kept, and being able to read it, even slowly, opens all of it to you.

How to learn it? The way most of the people in this book did: work out music you love by ear. Step is perfect for that, since step time lets you take as long as you like over every note. Pick a record, find its bass line one note at a time on Volt's keys, write it on Step, and play it against the record until it matches. Then the chords, then the drums. Do that for a dozen tracks and you'll have learned more than any chapter could teach you. A beginner's keyboard method, a good theory book or course, or lessons with someone who plays will take you further and faster. And remember house's rule: theory describes what people have found works. It doesn't forbid anything. If it sounds good, it is good.

12.4 An instrument for keeps

A Tessel is designed to go on being useful long after the last chapter of any book. Every unit can be reflashed as another kind whenever you like, and your sounds for each kind are kept, so a unit you bought for one job can do another next year and come back. New units snap on as you add them, one at a time, and the ones you have go on working with every new one. Everything you make is kept on the units themselves, and they make music without a computer. A Tessel doesn't need an account or a subscription, and it never will. It was made to be an instrument, and instruments are for keeps.

It isn't the only good instrument, and we'd be doing you no favours if we pretended it was. There are many other fine synthesisers, drum machines, samplers and grooveboxes, old and new, and a great deal of excellent music software, some of it free. Explore them. Every instrument pushes you in its own direction, and the ideas you've learned here, tracks and loops and mutes, filters and envelopes, chords and keys, work on all of them. We'd much rather you made music on anything at all than didn't make it.

12.5 With a computer, or without

Most electronic music today is made on a computer, in a DAW, a digital audio workstation: music software that records, sequences, edits and mixes everything, with synthesisers and effects inside it as software. What you've done in this book is the other way, often called DAW-less: hardware instruments, playing together, with no screen but their own. Neither is the right way. They're good at different things.

Without a computerWith a computer
Good atHands on real knobs; playing live; making decisions as you go and keeping them; no distractions on a screen; starting a track in secondsEditing every detail; unlimited tracks and undo; recording voices and instruments; mixing with precision; seeing the whole song at once
The catchLimits: so many units, so many tracks, a small screenEndless choice, which can be as paralysing as it is freeing; hours lost scrolling instead of playing

Limits are worth a second thought. Many musicians work without a computer precisely because of them: with fewer options you commit to a sound, a part or an arrangement and move on, and things get finished. Others want a computer for exactly what limits leave out: a singer's take, a guitar part, a perfect edit.

You don't have to choose for ever, or even for one track. A Tessel and a computer work together:

  • Recording. The Root's LINE OUT goes into a computer's audio interface, and any DAW records it. To record each unit on a track of its own, play the song once for each, with the others muted on Step's MIXER, and the DAW lines them up; then mix them there.
  • Playing in time together. Step's notes and clock go out of the Root's MIDI OUT (SETUP, ROOT, MIDI OUT), so a DAW listening on a MIDI input can follow Step's tempo. The other way, the Root's USB-C is a MIDI input from the computer (it carries no sound: that's LINE OUT's job), so a DAW's parts can play your units.
  • Sketching and finishing. Plenty of musicians start ideas on hardware, quickly and with their hands, and finish them on a computer, or play a computer-made track live with hardware on top.

12.6 A few things worth knowing

  • Finish things. A simple track finished teaches you more than ten brilliant loops left as loops. Give yourself a deadline, a week or an evening, and get to the end, even if the end isn't perfect. You'll do the next one better.
  • Listen on everything. A mix that's right on headphones can be wrong on a phone, in a car or on big speakers. Record your track, and play it on as many as you can before you call it done.
  • Share it. Play your tracks to friends, put them online, play them out. In Britain and most other countries, music you write is protected by copyright as soon as it's recorded, so it's yours; and remember section 6.1 about other people's.
  • Make music with other people. Join your MIDI to a friend's instruments, play to a singer, jam. Other people take your ideas somewhere you'd never have gone, and it's much more fun.
  • Look after your ears. Loud music damages hearing, slowly and for ever, and you'll want yours for the rest of your life. Keep headphones at a comfortable level and take breaks; if your ears ring after a session, it was too loud. Wear earplugs in clubs and at gigs: good musicians' earplugs make everything quieter without making it dull.
  • Keep listening. Every chapter's history named records to start with. Follow them: who influenced who, who sampled what, and the music next door, as chapter 7 did with the concert hall.

12.7 Last of all

The people who invented the music in this book didn't wait until they'd learned it all before they started: they learned by doing. Teenagers in Detroit and Chicago, kids in the Bronx and in London bedrooms, made it up with second-hand machines and whatever they had, copied what they loved, got it wrong in interesting ways and kept what worked. You have more help than they did, and better tools. The rest is yours. Make something nobody has heard before.

Quick reference

Every button, every page and every encoder on Step and Pilot.

For when you know what you want and just need to find it. Each map shows the unit's buttons as they sit on the panel, with the four boxes of each page in the corners where they'll appear on the screen: encoder 1 top left, 2 top right, 3 bottom left, 4 bottom right. A button with a second page shows it underneath (press the button again to get there). Under each map, a line on every control. Every synth's own pages are in Making Sounds' quick reference.

Every unit

SOUNDS the SOUNDS button
BANKwhich bank: FAC A... (the factory's) or USER A... (your own)
SOUNDwhich sound in it; it plays as soon as you reach it (on Strike: KIT)

NAMEyour own sounds: turn to change the letter, push for the next letter
THIS UNIT SETUP (the first pages)
MIDI CHthe unit's MIDI channel: AUTO, or one you choose (never changed after)
2-4the unit's own settings, listed under each unit below
RESET SETUP, the last THIS UNIT page
RESETencoder 1: SETTINGS, EVERYTHING, REFLASH (become another kind), another type kept in the unit's flash, EVERY TYPE, TOTAL RESET (wipe everything: a blank unit) or TEST (the unit's own test, then back as it was)
FIRMWAREthe firmware version; on REFLASH, BECOME: which kind, from the ones the Root carries
RESETencoder 4: hold for three seconds to do it
ROOT SETUP, after THIS UNIT (the Root's own settings)
INPUTwhich input units record from: LINE, MIC (with mic power) or BUILT-IN; also on Taste's and Grit's recording pages
GAINhow loud the input comes in, in dB; also on Taste's and Grit's recording pages
MIDI OUTOFF, NOTES (Step's), CLOCK (Step's tempo), BOTH, THRU (a copy of MIDI IN) or ALL

ROOT2 SETUP, the last page
MIDI INCHANNELS: each unit plays its own channel; FOLLOW: notes go to the unit last touched
FROM CHin FOLLOW, the channel the Root listens on
SOUNDSUNITS' (each kind's sounds from its leftmost unit) or ROOT'S: for a Root that already has sounds on it
KEEPencoder 4: hold for three seconds to do SOUNDS' choice
KEYBOARD while OCT- or OCT+ is held
OCTAVEmoves the keys by octaves (also: tap OCT- or OCT+)
SEMImoves the keys by semitones
LOWESTthe lowest note the keys now play
HIGHESTthe highest; press OCT- and OCT+ together to put them back

Step

Keys: on ENTRY and CHORD they write notes into the open track; elsewhere they play its unit. White keys light one bar of the open track (dim: a note, bright: the cursor, blinking: playing); black keys count the bar. OCT- and OCT+ move the keys and CHORD's chords by octaves. The left column works only on ENTRY and CHORD, and shows the note at the cursor.

ENTRY writing notes into the open track
LENGTH1/16T, 1/16, 1/8T, 1/8, 1/4T, 1/4, 1/2T, 1/2, 1; push: a rest; hold: a tie

BARmoves the cursor a LENGTH at a time; push: INSERT or REPLACE; hold: deletes the note at the cursor

LENGTHas ENTRY's
BARmoves the cursor; push: places the chord

TO TRACKCOPY: the track to copy to. TRANSPOSE: SEMITONES, -12 to +12. FILL: how many times
TOCOPY: where the copy starts. FILL: UNTIL, the last beat filled; push 2-4: sixteenths

hold anydoes it

Pilot

White keys: scenes. Press: every unit to the sound kept there; hold until the bar fills: keep every unit's sound there now (temporary edits aren't kept, and Pilot names the unit). Lit: the scene last called up; dim: keys with scenes. Black keys: not used. A knob can be any control on a sound unit's pages, any of Haze's effect settings or its MIX, or Step's TEMPO, SWING, MIXER levels and mutes, and track mutes.
